10.content:
Architecture decision records (ADRs) live in `docs/adr/` of the platform repository. Each summary
below links to the full record.

11.content:
**Accepted.** Templates are shared across tenants, but each tenant has its own cloud accounts. So
the provider, account and region cannot live in the template.

12.content:
Instead, a template declares **placement slots**, each with a list of allowed providers. Every
resource names a slot, and every instance binds each slot to `{ targetId, region }`. The same
template runs on one cloud or on several, depending only on the bindings. Networks bind only to
resources in the same slot.
Read ADR 0001

13.content:
**Accepted.** `CloudProviderAdapter` is the only way the platform touches a cloud. Its
`ensureResource` call converges a resource to the desired state, so a retry cannot create a
duplicate.

14.content:
The mapping from a logical resource to a provider implementation is **data**: capability catalogs
that list features, regional gaps and static prices. A deterministic `mock` provider simulates
AWS, Azure or OCI with injectable failures, and the platform labels everything it simulates. One
shared contract test suite runs against every adapter.
Read ADR 0002

15.content:
**Accepted.** Temporal would add a cluster to operate. BullMQ reuses the Redis and Postgres that
the platform already requires.

16.content:
A job carries only the deployment id. Steps are database rows, created when the deployment is
requested and updated before and after each action. Resuming a deployment means running the same
job again, which skips the phases that already finished. Temporal is worth another look if long
flows that wait on people, or very large fan out, appear.
Read ADR 0003

17.content:
**Accepted.** All tenants share one database, and every row a tenant owns carries a `tenantId`.
Isolation works in four layers: the request principal, query scoping by membership, a CASL check
on the loaded record, and the audit log. A record from another tenant is reported as not found.

18.content:
CASL rules are defined once. The API enforces them, and the console receives them only to decide
what to show. Sessions are opaque and stored on the server, not JWTs. OIDC providers are plain
configuration.
Read ADR 0004

19.content:
**Accepted.** Every `tofu` command runs in a throwaway container with a pinned image. Credentials
exist only in that container's environment.

20.content:
Each resource has **its own state file** in S3, locked with `use_lockfile` and encrypted. This keeps
the platform's own DAG and isolates a failure to one resource. State holds no secrets: passwords
come from ephemeral resources and travel through write only attributes. The same code serves real
AWS and MiniStack.
Read ADR 0005

82.content: The CI checks that run on OrkStage today, and the planned release flow for images, packages, signed CLI binaries, modules and this site.

86.content:
OrkStage is developed on `main` and has not published a versioned release. This page lists the
checks that run today and the release flow being prepared.

87.content:
| Repository part                       | Checks                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Platform (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) | `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, build, type check and tests. Migrations apply cleanly on Postgres, and the seed runs twice to prove it is idempotent. `pnpm audit --audit-level high` reports vulnerable dependencies but does not fail the build yet. |

88.content:
| Repository part                      | Checks                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| CLI (`cli/.github/workflows/ci.yml`) | `cargo fmt`, `clippy -D warnings` and tests on Linux, macOS and Windows. The committed WASM package must match a fresh build and pass a smoke test. Release builds run for 8 targets. On tags, and only when the signing secrets are configured, Windows binaries get Authenticode signatures and macOS binaries get Developer ID signing and notarization. |

89.content:
**Versioning.** Each repository uses semantic versions. A breaking API change gets a new
`/api/v2` route group. The template schema has its own version (`platform/v1`).

90.content:
**Platform.** A tag builds and publishes `ghcr.io/orkstage/platform:<version>` and the shared
packages (`@orkstage/contracts`, `/authorization`, `/templates` and `/domain`). The exported
OpenAPI document is attached to the release.

91.content:
**Console.** A tag publishes `ghcr.io/orkstage/console:<version>`, pinned to a compatible range
of the contracts package.

92.content:
**CLI.** A tag publishes signed `ork` binaries for Linux (glibc and musl), macOS and Windows on
`x86_64` and `arm64`, then `@orkstage/scan` on npm, then manifests for Homebrew, Scoop and
winget.

93.content:
**Modules.** Git tags `vX.Y.Z` publish `ghcr.io/orkstage/tofu-runner:<tag>`. The platform pins
the runner tag, so a module change is always an explicit upgrade.

94.content:
**Compatibility matrix.** `orkstage-dev/COMPATIBILITY.md` lists the combination of versions
that was tested together. Its CI runs the end to end suite against that combination.

95.content:
**Site.** This site refreshes the API reference from the release's OpenAPI file and deploys to
S3 and CloudFront.

96.content:
Each repository will keep a changelog per release. Security fixes ship as patch versions. The plan
is for Enterprise customers to receive security advisories before public disclosure.

139.content: Create, use, scope and revoke OrkStage API keys for CI/CD, scripts and the ork CLI. Token format, roles, the ten scopes, expiry, auditing and storage.

147.content:
API keys authenticate automation: CI pipelines, scripts and the `ork` CLI. Each key acts with a
**role**, and its **scopes** narrow what that role allows. A key can never do more than its role,
and no key can manage other keys.

148.content: `env` is `live` or `test`. It is a label for you, and both kinds work the same way.

149.content:
The prefix (`ork_<env>_` plus 8 hex characters, for example `ork_live_7f3a9c21`) is stored and
appears in key lists and audit entries.

150.content:
The server stores only the SHA-256 hash of the full token. You see the token **once**, when you
create the key.

151.content:
Open **Integrations**, then **API keys**, then **New API key**. Pick a preset or choose the scopes
yourself:

156.content: Copy the token right away and put it in your CI secret store.

157.content: Only a signed in user (a session) can create keys. Another key cannot:

158.content:
| Key        | `tenantId` | Allowed roles                                          | Who can create it                                            |
| ---------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Tenant key | required   | `CustomerAdmin`, `CustomerDeveloper`, `CustomerViewer` | Owners and admins of that tenant, platform owners and admins |

159.content:
| Key              | `tenantId` | Allowed roles                       | Who can create it               |
| ---------------- | ---------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Organization key | omitted    | `PlatformAdmin`, `PlatformOperator` | Platform owners and admins only |

160.content:
The API rejects any other combination with `INVALID_KEY_ROLE`, `TENANT_REQUIRED` or
`ROLE_TOO_HIGH`.

161.content:
Templates and catalog applications are shared by all tenants, so only platform roles can change
them. Creating or publishing a template (`ork template push`, or a template from an import) and
registering or publishing application images need an organization key with the `PlatformAdmin`
role. A tenant key can still validate templates, create imports and deploy.

172.content:
When a key lacks the scope an endpoint requires, the API answers `403 API_KEY_SCOPE` and names the
required scope in `details`. An endpoint that declares no scope answers `403 API_KEY_NOT_ALLOWED`.

173.content: Requests with a bearer token need no `x-orkstage-csrf` header.

174.content:
**Expiry**: `expiresAt` is optional and must be in the future. An expired key gets
`401 INVALID_API_KEY`.

175.content:
**Revocation**: call `DELETE /api/v1/api-keys/:id` (it returns `204`) or use the console. The key
stops working at once and also gets `401 INVALID_API_KEY`.

176.content: **Last use**: the API updates `lastUsedAt` and the client address at most once a minute.

177.content:
**Audit**: every action a key takes is recorded with `actorType = API_KEY` and
`actorLabel = "<key name> (<prefix>)"`.

178.content: Create one key per pipeline or integration, with the smallest preset that works.

179.content: Prefer tenant keys with `CustomerDeveloper` over organization keys where the job allows it.

180.content: Set an expiry. To rotate, create the new key first and then revoke the old one.

182.content: How the OrkStage Control API v1 works. Base path, API keys and sessions, the CSRF header, errors, pagination, correlation ids, idempotency and rate limits.

192.content:
The Control API is the only way into the platform, and the console uses it too. The base path is
**`/api/v1`**. A running API serves an OpenAPI UI at `/api/docs` and the OpenAPI document at
`/api/docs-json`. The API reference in these docs is generated from
that document.

193.content:
Send an API key as a bearer token. You need no cookie and no CSRF
header.

194.content:
A key reaches only the endpoints that declare a scope. Endpoints without a scope, such as API key
management, answer `403 API_KEY_NOT_ALLOWED` to a key.

195.content:
The console signs in through OIDC (or the development login when you run locally) and receives an
opaque session token in the `orkstage_session` cookie. The cookie is `httpOnly` and `SameSite=Lax`, is
`Secure` in production, and expires after 12 hours. The server stores only the SHA-256 hash of the
token, and logout revokes it.

196.content:
Every request that changes state (`POST`, `PATCH`, `PUT`, `DELETE`) and uses a session must send
this header:

197.content:
A browser cannot add a custom header to a request for another site without a CORS preflight, and the
API allows no CORS requests from other origins. Other sites therefore cannot forge requests.

198.content:
`GET /me` returns the caller, their memberships and the authorization rules. When you call it with an
API key, it also returns `apiKey: { id, name, prefix, scopes }`.

199.content: Error responses never contain stack traces. They all have this shape:

200.content:
| Status | Typical codes                                            |
| ------ | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| 400    | `VALIDATION_ERROR`, with the failing fields in `details` |

203.content:
| Status | Typical codes                                                               |
| ------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 402    | `ENTERPRISE_REQUIRED` (an Enterprise feature and no license that covers it) |

205.content:
| Status | Typical codes                                     |
| ------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
| 404    | Not found, **including records of other tenants** |

208.content:
| Status | Typical codes                                                         |
| ------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 501    | `SCANNER_UNAVAILABLE` (the API was built without the IaC scan engine) |

209.content:
Send `x-correlation-id` to tie your logs to ours. Every response carries `x-correlation-id` and
`x-request-id`. The correlation id follows the request into deployments, OpenTofu runs, audit events
and webhook deliveries, so quote it when you report a problem.

210.content: List endpoints that can grow use cursors and return the newest items first:

212.content:
Deploy and destroy return **`202 Accepted`** with a deployment summary. The work never runs inside the
request. Follow its progress with these endpoints:

213.content:
You can also subscribe to webhooks for `deployment.succeeded`,
`deployment.failed` and `deployment.awaiting_approval`.

214.content:
Deployments are keyed by tenant, instance and a hash of the desired state. While an instance has an
operation in progress, further deploy or destroy requests get `409 INSTANCE_BUSY`, and the worker
never recreates resources that have already converged. The API accepts an `Idempotency-Key` header
but ignores it for now.

215.content:
Reads of tenant records are filtered by the caller's memberships, and every write is checked against
the record loaded from the database. The API never trusts a `tenantId` in a request on its own.

458.content:
Every image version belongs to an application in the catalog. Create the application from the
pipeline before the first publish. The call is idempotent: the same body sent again changes nothing,
so you can run it on every build.

459.content:
A name has 2 to 63 characters: lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starting with a letter.
Other names get `422 INVALID_NAME`.

461.content:
The response contains `"created": true` the first time. Every change is audited as `CREATE` or
`UPDATE` on `Application`.

462.content:
The catalog is shared by all tenants, so the call needs an organization key with the
`PlatformAdmin` role and the `applications:write` scope.

463.content:
Templates refer to images through the application catalog (`image: catalog://orders-api`). When
OrkStage compiles an instance, each reference resolves to the **most recently published version** of
that application, by digest. A deployment therefore always runs an immutable image.

464.content: `digest` must be `sha256:` followed by 64 lowercase hex characters.

466.content:
Versions are immutable. Publishing a version again with the **same** digest is idempotent (the
response has `"idempotent": true`). With a different digest it fails with `409 VERSION_EXISTS`.

467.content: Every publish is audited as `PUBLISH` on `ApplicationVersion`.

468.content:
Publishing needs the same organization key as registration: role `PlatformAdmin`, scope
`applications:write`.

469.content: The validation endpoint is stateless. It needs no template id and stores nothing.

470.content: The report lists every issue with its `stage`, `severity`, `code`, `message` and `path`.

471.content:
If you deploy while another operation is running, the API answers `409 INSTANCE_BUSY`. Treat it as
"try again later", not as a failed build.

472.content:
To keep publishing and deploying apart, use two keys: an organization key with the **Image
publishing** preset for the publish step, and a tenant key with the **CI/CD deploy** preset for the
deploy step.

487.content:
`ork` turns an existing project into an OrkStage template, pushes it, and deploys and operates
instances from your terminal or from CI. It reads Terraform and OpenTofu, CloudFormation, SAM and
CDK, Kubernetes and Helm, Docker Compose, Dockerfiles and package manifests. It also detects Pulumi,
Serverless, Bicep and ARM projects. The CLI is written in Rust and licensed under AGPL-3.0.

`SHA256SUMS` and install it without administrator rights.

release on GitHub also has the archives and
`SHA256SUMS` for a manual install.

The CLI stores one key per API URL in the OS keychain: macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager,
or Secret Service on Linux. Where no keychain is available (containers, CI runners without a
desktop session), it writes them to `credentials.toml` (mode 0600) in the user config directory:

549.content: Keys are never written to the project.

550.content:
**Walk** (CLI only). A parallel walk that respects `.gitignore` skips `node_modules`,
`.terraform`, `target`, `vendor`, `dist`, hidden directories and CDK `asset.*` copies. It also
skips files over 1 MiB (configurable) and files that are not valid UTF-8.

551.content:
**Detect** each source kind. Terraform is parsed as HCL. The scan evaluates `var.*`, `local.*`
and simple expressions, expands local modules per call and reports remote modules as unmapped.
References such as `aws_db_instance.main.address` in a task definition become connections.
CloudFormation tags in short form (such as `!Ref`, `!GetAtt` and `!Sub`) are normalized.

552.content:
**Merge**. When several sources show the same component, it becomes one resource that keeps
every source. IaC evidence wins over Kubernetes, and Kubernetes wins over Compose, Dockerfiles and
package hints.

553.content:
**Infer**. The scan adds a network when services or data stores need one, and an ingress plus DNS
for a public HTTP service on a cloud provider. It then chooses placement slots and the smallest
plan whose default entitlements fit.

554.content:
**Render and validate** the template. Problems become warnings, so the scan never fails on bad
input.

555.content:
In the generated template, each image is a catalog reference named after its service
(`catalog://api`). The resource's `sourceImage` property keeps the image the scan detected.

557.content: How the IaC import API and scan engine work. Supported sources, mapping rules, the ScanReport v1 format and the calls that create a draft template.

566.content:
An import turns infrastructure code into a **draft template** that you review. One engine,
`orkstage-scan` (written in Rust), does all detection and mapping. The `ork` CLI runs it natively,
and the platform runs it compiled to WebAssembly (`@orkstage/scan`).

567.content:
| Path                                                                                 | Status    |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------- |
| `POST /imports { report }`: send a ScanReport produced by `ork import` or `ork scan` | Available |

568.content:
| Path                                                                 | Status                                                                                                                               |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `POST /imports { files }`: upload files and let the server scan them | Available. The API ships with the scan engine (`@orkstage/scan`, WebAssembly). A build without it answers `501 SCANNER_UNAVAILABLE`. |

569.content:
| Path                                       | Status  |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------- |
| `ork import` or `ork scan` on your machine | Preview |

570.content:
| Source kind | What the engine reads                                                             |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `terraform` | `.tf` and `.tf.json` files; variables, locals, local modules, resource references |

571.content:
| Source kind                    | What the engine reads                                                           |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `cloudformation`, `sam`, `cdk` | Templates in YAML or JSON, including tags in short form; synthesized CDK output |

572.content:
| Source kind          | What the engine reads                                        |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `kubernetes`, `helm` | Deployments, Services, Ingresses, StatefulSets; `Chart.yaml` |

573.content:
| Source kind | What the engine reads                                                              |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `compose`   | Services, ports, images and dependencies in `docker-compose.yml` or `compose.yaml` |

574.content:
| Source kind  | What the engine reads         |
| ------------ | ----------------------------- |
| `dockerfile` | Base images and exposed ports |

575.content:
| Source kind | What the engine reads                                                                                    |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `package`   | `package.json`, `go.mod`, `requirements.txt` and similar files, as hints (for example a Postgres driver) |

576.content:
| Source kind                            | What the engine reads |
| -------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| `pulumi`, `serverless`, `bicep`, `arm` | Detected and reported |

577.content:
Detected resources map to the nine OrkStage types: `network`, `compute.container-service`,
`container-registry`, `database.postgresql`, `cache.redis`, `queue`, `object-storage`, `ingress` and
`dns`. Anything else appears in the **unmapped** list with a reason. Nothing is dropped silently.

578.content:
When several sources show the same component, it becomes **one** resource that keeps every
source. For example, a Compose `postgres` service, `pg` in `package.json` and an
`aws_db_instance` become one `database.postgresql` on AWS.

579.content:
Evidence strength, from strongest: IaC, then Kubernetes, then Compose, Dockerfiles and package
hints.

580.content:
References become **connections**, for example a task definition that reads
`aws_db_instance.main.address`.

581.content:
The engine adds a network when services or data stores need one. It adds an ingress and DNS when a
public HTTP service runs on a cloud provider.

582.content:
Placement slots are chosen per provider: `primary` for the compute provider, and slots such as
`data`, `storage` and `messaging` for the others. The engine also picks the smallest plan whose
default entitlements fit.

583.content: Each resource has a **confidence** of `high`, `medium` or `low`.

584.content: To let the server scan the files instead, send them as text:

585.content:
Send **either** `files` (text only, at most 2000 files and 5 MB in total) **or** `report`, never
both. The response is an `ImportDto`:

586.content: A report that is not a ScanReport version 1 gets `422 INVALID_REPORT`.

728.content: Receive signed OrkStage events over HTTPS. Event types, payload, signature checks in Node.js, Python and Go, retries, testing and redelivery.

735.content:
OrkStage sends events to your HTTPS endpoints as JSON `POST` requests signed with HMAC-SHA256. Use
them to post to chat, open tickets, start pipelines or feed your incident tools.

736.content:
| Event                | When                               |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `deployment.started` | The worker picked up a deployment. |

737.content:
| Event                  | When                                      |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `deployment.succeeded` | A deployment (apply or destroy) finished. |

738.content:
| Event               | When                           |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `deployment.failed` | A deployment ended in failure. |

739.content:
| Event                          | When                                                  |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `deployment.awaiting_approval` | A high risk production deployment waits for approval. |

740.content:
| Event               | When                          |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| `instance.degraded` | An instance's health dropped. |

741.content:
| Event                     | When                                                |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `instance.drift_detected` | The drift scan found changes made outside OrkStage. |

742.content:
| Event                                                      | When                                         |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `incident.opened`, `incident.updated`, `incident.resolved` | An incident was opened, updated or resolved. |

743.content:
| Event                    | When                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `cloud_target.unhealthy` | A cloud target failed validation, either when someone validates it or when a deployment checks it before it starts. Sent once, when the target becomes unhealthy. |

744.content:
| Event  | When                                                                                                     |
| ------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ping` | Sent by the **Test** button in the console and by `POST /webhooks/:id/test`. You cannot subscribe to it. |

745.content:
In the console, open **Integrations**, then **Webhooks**, then **New webhook**. Through the API, use a
session or a key with `webhooks:manage`:

746.content:
The response contains `{ webhook, secret }`. You see the signing secret (`whsec_…`) **once**. The
server stores it encrypted with `ENCRYPTION_KEY`. To rotate it, call
`POST /webhooks/:id/rotate-secret`, which returns the new secret.

747.content:
OrkStage checks the URL when you create the endpoint and again before every delivery, because DNS
can change:

748.content: The URL must use `https://` and must not contain credentials.

749.content: The host must not resolve to a private, loopback, link local or multicast address.

750.content: Redirects are not followed, and each request times out after 10 seconds.

751.content:
For local development, `WEBHOOK_ALLOW_PRIVATE=true` also accepts `http://` URLs and private
addresses. The API refuses to start with this setting in production.

752.content:
`OrkStage-Delivery` is unique per delivery and stays the same across retries. A manual redelivery is
a new delivery with a new `OrkStage-Delivery` value, but its body keeps the original `id`. To drop
duplicates, use the body `id`, which covers both retries and redeliveries.

753.content: Read the **raw** request body, before any JSON parsing.

754.content: Split the header on `,` and `=` to get `t` and `v1`.

755.content:
Reject the request if `t` is more than **300 seconds** away from your clock. This protects
against replays.

756.content:
Compute `HMAC-SHA256(secret, t + "." + rawBody)` as lowercase hex and compare it with `v1` in
constant time.

757.content: Answer with a `2xx` status quickly, and do the work in the background.

758.content: The platform uses the same algorithm in `verifyWebhook` (`packages/runtime/src/webhooks.ts`).

761.content:
|                     |                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Automatic disabling | After 20 failed deliveries in a row, OrkStage disables the endpoint and records a reason. Turn it back on with `PATCH /webhooks/:id { "enabled": true }`, which also resets the failure count. |

762.content:
| Endpoint                  | What it does                                            |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `POST /webhooks/:id/test` | Sends a `ping` at once and returns the delivery result. |

763.content:
| Endpoint                       | What it does                                                                   |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `GET /webhooks/:id/deliveries` | Lists the last 50 deliveries with status, attempts, response status and error. |

764.content:
| Endpoint                                              | What it does                                                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `POST /webhooks/:id/deliveries/:deliveryId/redeliver` | Creates a new delivery with the same payload and answers `202`. The worker sends it on its next pass. |

765.content:
| Endpoint              | What it does                                         |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `PATCH /webhooks/:id` | Changes `url`, `description`, `events` or `enabled`. |

766.content:
| Endpoint               | What it does          |
| ---------------------- | --------------------- |
| `DELETE /webhooks/:id` | Removes the endpoint. |

767.content:
In the console, open **Integrations**, then **Webhooks**. The **Deliveries** button of an endpoint
lists its recent deliveries, each with a **Redeliver** button.

795.content: OrkStage Enterprise adds identity, governance and compliance features to the open source core. Same code and images, turned on by an offline license key.

798.content:
OrkStage is **open core**. The Community edition, under the GNU AGPL-3.0, is the complete control
plane. You can run it on your own infrastructure and use it for production workloads on AWS without
paying anyone.

799.content:
Enterprise adds what larger and regulated organizations need around the core: identity integration,
finer governance, compliance exports, several organizations and support with an SLA.

800.content:
**One codebase, one build.** Enterprise code lives in directories named `ee/` and ships in the
same images. There is no separate fork.

801.content:
**A license key turns it on.** Set `ORKSTAGE_LICENSE_KEY` to the key you receive. The key is a
signed token (Ed25519) that OrkStage verifies **offline**. OrkStage does not contact a license
server and does not require usage reports.

802.content:
**Your data stays usable.** Without a key, or with an invalid key, OrkStage runs as Community. When
a key expires, a banner shows a 14 day grace period, after which Enterprise features switch off.
OrkStage never deletes or locks your data.

803.content:
**A clear boundary.** Core code never imports from `ee/`. Enterprise features plug into extension
points. Without a license that covers them, gated endpoints answer `402 ENTERPRISE_REQUIRED`.

804.content:
**Edition at a glance.** `GET /api/v1/license` reports the active edition and features, and the
console shows an edition badge.

805.content:

843.content: The OrkStage vocabulary, from instances, templates and placement slots to cloud targets, plans, deployments, health, incidents and audit.

856.content:
An **organization** runs one OrkStage installation. It serves **tenants**, the customers or teams
that own instances. Every record that belongs to a tenant carries its tenant id. A user sees a
tenant only through a membership with one of the roles. Each tenant is
on a **plan**.

857.content:
An **instance**, also called a **stage**, is one isolated, logical environment for one tenant. It
holds the services, database, cache, queue, storage, ingress and DNS, for example *Acme Production*
or *Acme Staging*. Each instance has an environment kind (`production`, `staging`, `development` or
`sandbox`), a template version, variable values and one placement binding per slot.

858.content: The instance status follows a state machine, and every transition is validated:

859.content:
The failed states are `VALIDATION_FAILED`, `PLAN_FAILED`, `PROVISION_FAILED`, `DEPLOY_FAILED` (also
from `CONFIGURING`) and `VERIFICATION_FAILED`. A rejected approval ends in `PLAN_FAILED`, and a
destroy cancelled before anything was deleted returns the instance to `READY`.

860.content:
Only one operation runs on an instance at a time. A second deploy or destroy gets
`409 INSTANCE_BUSY`.

861.content:
A **template** (`apiVersion: platform/v1`, `kind: EnvironmentTemplate`) describes business intent,
never provider resource blocks. Examples: "a container service with two replicas", "a Postgres
database spread across availability zones", "private connectivity from api to database".

862.content:
Templates are versioned. A published version never changes, and an instance moves to a new version
only through an explicit upgrade. OrkStage ships six templates, from `free-validation` to
`multicloud-reference`. See the template reference.

863.content:
A **cloud target** is an account you register with a provider: an AWS account, an Azure
subscription or an OCI tenancy. It stores the allowed regions and configuration that is not secret.
Credentials are stored as references, never as values.

864.content:
A template declares **placement slots** such as `primary`, `data` and `storage`, and lists the
providers each slot accepts. Every resource names a slot, and an instance binds each slot to a target
and a region. Bind all slots to one AWS account and the template runs on a single cloud. Bind `data`
to Azure and the same template becomes multicloud.

866.content:
Most organizations keep production, staging and development in separate accounts of the same
provider. Register one target per account, each with its own credentials, and set the environment
it serves: `production`, `staging`, `development` or `sandbox`. An instance can only deploy into
targets of its own environment; the `target-environment` policy stops a production instance from
landing in a development account, and a development instance from touching production. Mark a
target `any` only when it is meant for every environment, such as the simulation targets.

870.content: Target names are unique within a tenant (and among shared targets), ignoring case.

871.content:
Mark one target per provider and environment as the **default** (in the console, or
`POST /api/v1/cloud/targets/{id}/default`). When an instance is created with a slot left unbound,
in the console, the API or `ork instances create` with that slot missing from `[placements]`,
OrkStage binds the slot to the default target of the instance's environment (the tenant's own before
a shared one, the exact environment before `any`, then the order of providers the slot accepts). The
binding is stored with the instance, so changing the default later never moves existing instances.

872.content:
Each provider adapter publishes a **capability catalog**. For each logical resource type, it lists
the concrete service that implements it, with its features, regional gaps and static list prices.
For example, `database.postgresql` maps to `rds-postgres` on AWS, `flexible-server` on Azure and
`oci-postgresql` on OCI. The resolver picks the default, or the `implementation` the template
prefers, and suggests alternatives when nothing fits.

873.content:
| Logical type | AWS | Azure (Preview) | OCI (Preview) |
| ------------ | --- | --------------- | ------------- |
| `network`    | VPC | Virtual Network | VCN           |

874.content:

| --------------------------- | -------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------- |
| `compute.container-service` | ECS on Fargate, ECS on EC2 | Container Apps  | Container Instances |

| -------------------- | --- | ------------------ | ------------------ |
| `container-registry` | ECR | Container Registry | Not in the catalog |

| --------------------- | ------------------ | -------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| `database.postgresql` | RDS for PostgreSQL | PostgreSQL Flexible Server | Database with PostgreSQL |

882.content:
A tenant's **plan** (`FREE`, `SANDBOX`, `STARTER`, `GROWTH` or `SCALE`) grants **entitlements**.
Some are limits: instances, services, CPU, memory, storage, replicas, domains and retention. Others
are switches: custom templates, custom cloud accounts, several regions, several clouds and
autoscaling.

883.content:
A template lists the plans it supports. The compiler refuses a placement the plan does not allow,
for example a second provider when `multiCloud` is off.

884.content:
| Plan | Instances | Multicloud | Multiple regions | Custom templates |
| ---- | --------- | ---------- | ---------------- | ---------------- |
| FREE | 1         | no         | no               | no               |

885.content:
| Plan    | Instances | Multicloud | Multiple regions | Custom templates |
| ------- | --------- | ---------- | ---------------- | ---------------- |
| SANDBOX | 2         | no         | no               | no               |

886.content:
| Plan    | Instances | Multicloud | Multiple regions | Custom templates |
| ------- | --------- | ---------- | ---------------- | ---------------- |
| STARTER | 3         | no         | no               | no               |

887.content:
| Plan   | Instances | Multicloud | Multiple regions | Custom templates |
| ------ | --------- | ---------- | ---------------- | ---------------- |
| GROWTH | 10        | yes        | no               | yes              |

888.content:
| Plan  | Instances | Multicloud | Multiple regions | Custom templates |
| ----- | --------- | ---------- | ---------------- | ---------------- |
| SCALE | 100       | yes        | yes              | yes              |

889.content:
These values are the defaults that ship with OrkStage. The copy in the database is the one that
applies.

890.content: When you preview an instance, OrkStage compiles the template into a **resolved infrastructure**:

892.content: each resource bound to a target, a region and a capability;

895.content: a connectivity strategy for each link;

896.content: a policy report and an approximate cost.

897.content:
A diff against the known resources gives the **deployment plan** (create, update, delete,
unchanged) and its risk. This step never touches a cloud. The deployment stores a snapshot of the
plan, so OrkStage applies exactly what you previewed. See
Reviewing plan & cost.

898.content:
A **deployment** applies a plan in the background. The worker runs fixed phases: validate, targets,
plan, approval (when needed), resources, rollout, configure, verify, observability and finalize.

899.content:
Resources are provisioned in dependency order, and independent branches run in parallel. The worker
retries transient failures with backoff. A failed resource blocks only the resources that depend on
it. After a worker crash, the deployment resumes where it stopped. See
Deploying and watching progress.

900.content:
The database holds the **desired** state (template and configuration) and the **known** state (what
OrkStage recorded). The provider holds the **actual** state. Each resource carries a knowledge
state (`DESIRED`, `KNOWN`, `ACTUAL` or `UNKNOWN`) and a drift status.

901.content:
OrkStage checks health (`HEALTHY`, `DEGRADED`, `UNHEALTHY`, `UNKNOWN` or `MAINTENANCE`) on each
resource and rolls it up to the instance. An unhealthy critical component makes the instance
unhealthy. Any other problem makes it degraded.

902.content:
Resources map to **status components** that customers see, such as API, Workers and Database, on a
private **status page**. Alert rules open **incidents**, deduplicated per resource and subject to a
cooldown. An incident resolves on its own when health returns. **Notifications** go to
the console, to email and to signed webhooks.

903.content:
Every action that changes state writes an **audit event** with the actor (user or API key), tenant,
resource, action, correlation id and changes. The audit table only accepts inserts. A Postgres
trigger enforces this.

905.content: OrkStage is an open source multicloud control plane. Define an environment once, place each resource on a cloud, review the plan and deploy with OpenTofu.

909.content:
OrkStage provisions and operates **isolated environments** on one or several clouds. Each
environment is called an *instance* (or a *stage*). It is a logical unit that groups services, a
Postgres database, a cache, a queue, object storage, ingress and DNS.

910.content:
**OrkStage places each resource on its own.** One instance can run its API on AWS, its database on
Azure and its storage on OCI.

911.content: Every instance follows the same flow:

912.content:
A **template** describes what the environment needs, without naming a provider. You write it
once and deploy it many times.

913.content: An **instance** binds each placement slot of the template to a cloud target and a region.

914.content:
The **plan** resolves every resource, evaluates policies, estimates the monthly cost and picks a
connectivity strategy for each link between clouds. No cloud is touched at this step.

915.content: A **deployment** applies the plan in the background with OpenTofu, following the dependency graph.

916.content:
**Health checks** roll up to the instance. They open **incidents**, update a private **status
page** and send **notifications**. Every change is recorded in an **audit log** that only accepts
inserts.

917.content:
OrkStage provisions real AWS resources with OpenTofu. We test this locally against
MiniStack, and it works on a real account through a role that OrkStage
assumes in that account. Azure, Google Cloud, OCI, DigitalOcean, Vultr, CoreWeave, Magalu Cloud,
Vercel, Render and Supabase have adapters in Preview: covered by tests and
`tofu validate`, not yet proven on live accounts (see providers). The
simulation provider imitates any of them without an account and labels its resources as
simulated. The `ork` CLI is in Preview: it works against the API, but signed
binaries are not released yet.

926.content:
**Platform and DevOps teams** that run the same environment shape for many customers or teams.
They get one reviewed path from template to cloud, with policy checks on every plan.

927.content:
**SREs** who need health, incidents, status and an audit trail tied to the infrastructure that
was actually deployed.

928.content:
**Engineering managers** who approve production changes. They see the plan, the risk and an
approximate cost before anything is created.

929.content:
The core is licensed under the GNU **AGPL-3.0** and is complete on its own. You can run it on your
own infrastructure and use it for production workloads on AWS. Directories named `ee/` hold
Enterprise features under a commercial license, which an offline license key turns on. See
Community vs Enterprise.

931.content: Provision real AWS resources with OpenTofu against MiniStack, a local emulator that runs real ECS, RDS and ElastiCache containers. No AWS account needed.

941.content:
MiniStack is an AWS emulator under the MIT license. Most API mocks only
answer calls; MiniStack also starts real containers for ECS tasks, RDS and ElastiCache. A deployment
against it runs the same OpenTofu modules, the same state handling and the same health checks as a
deployment against a real account.

942.content:
MiniStack needs the Docker socket to start those containers, which gives it control of your Docker
daemon. Use it on a development machine only.

943.content:
The quickstart compose command already includes the `aws-emulator`
profile. If you run the apps on the host instead, start MiniStack on its own:

944.content:
MiniStack listens on `http://localhost:4566`. Inside the compose network its address is
`http://ministack:4566`, and the containers it starts join the same network.

945.content: The seed registers an AWS cloud target named **Local AWS (MiniStack)**:

946.content:
| Field      | Meaning                                                                    |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `emulator` | Switches to the emulator's static test credentials and endpoint overrides. |

947.content:
| Field         | Meaning                                                    |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `endpointUrl` | The AWS endpoint as the API and worker processes reach it. |

948.content:
| Field               | Meaning                                                   |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `runnerEndpointUrl` | The same endpoint as OpenTofu runner containers reach it. |

949.content:
| Field                      | Meaning                                                                                           |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `dnsZone`, `createDnsZone` | The platform DNS zone for instance subdomains. On the emulator, OrkStage creates it on first use. |

950.content:
In the compose stack, the worker also sets `AWS_EMULATOR_ENDPOINT=http://ministack:4566`. Links in
the console keep `http://localhost:4566`, so your browser can open them.

951.content:
Open **Cloud targets**, then **Local AWS (MiniStack)**, and click **Validate**. Validation checks the
emulator credentials, account access and the OpenTofu state bucket. On the emulator, OrkStage
creates the bucket and turns on versioning the first time it needs it. Validation fails with a clear
message when MiniStack is not running. The IAM permission probe runs on real accounts only.

952.content:
Open **Instances**, then **Acme Staging (local AWS)** (template `starter-standard`), and click
**Deploy**. The worker runs one OpenTofu container per resource step, in dependency order. Each
resource gets its own state file in MiniStack's S3.

953.content:
| Template resource | AWS resources (OpenTofu module)                                                                                 |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `network`         | VPC, public and private subnets, internet gateway, route tables, internal security group (optional NAT gateway) |

954.content:
| Template resource | AWS resources (OpenTofu module)                                         |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `registry`        | ECR repository with scan on push, immutable tags and a lifecycle policy |

955.content:
| Template resource | AWS resources (OpenTofu module)                                                                   |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `database`        | RDS PostgreSQL instance, subnet group, security group, Secrets Manager secret for the credentials |

956.content:
| Template resource | AWS resources (OpenTofu module)                                    |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `cache`           | ElastiCache Valkey replication group, subnet group, security group |

957.content:
| Template resource | AWS resources (OpenTofu module)                                                      |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `messaging`       | SQS queue, plus a second queue for messages that fail processing (dead letter queue) |

958.content:
| Template resource | AWS resources (OpenTofu module)                                                             |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `api`, `worker`   | ECS cluster, task definition, service, CloudWatch log group, execution role, security group |

959.content:

| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ingress`         | Application Load Balancer, target groups, HTTP listener and path rules |

960.content:

| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |

961.content:
MiniStack serves the ALB at `http://localhost:4566/_alb/<lb-name>/`. The console shows this address
as the `url` output of the ingress.

962.content:
You can bind only the `primary` slot of `multicloud-reference` to MiniStack and keep `data` (Azure)
and `storage` (OCI) on the simulated targets. OrkStage provisions the AWS part for real. The rest is
simulated and labelled as simulated.

963.content:
On a second plan, MiniStack reports changes in place for some RDS and ElastiCache attributes. Drift
scans against the emulator can therefore flag changes nobody made. Treat drift on MiniStack as a
hint.

964.content:
MiniStack does not emulate autoscaling. Services run their fixed `replicas`, and the deployment
logs a warning.

965.content:
MiniStack does not serve the public SSM parameter for the Amazon ECS optimized AMI. On the
emulator, `ecs-ec2` services use a placeholder AMI.

966.content:
This command runs the contract suite of the AWS provider adapter (ensure, read, health, delete)
against MiniStack.

968.content: Run the full OrkStage platform locally with Docker Compose, sign in with the development login and deploy your first instance in about ten minutes.

978.content: Alternative: run the apps on the host

980.content:
This guide runs everything in containers: the API, the worker, the console, Postgres, Redis, a mail
catcher, the OpenTofu runner image and MiniStack (a local AWS emulator). **Docker is the only
requirement.** You need no cloud account and no Node.js on the host.

981.content:
The compose stack runs with `NODE_ENV=development`. The development login is on, cookies are not
`Secure`, and the worker mounts the Docker socket to start OpenTofu containers. Do not expose this
stack to a network. For production, see Docker Compose deployment
and Security hardening.

982.content:
Docker Engine or Docker Desktop with Compose v2, and about 6 GB of free memory for the full stack.
MiniStack starts real containers for RDS, ElastiCache and ECS tasks.

984.content:
`orkstage-dev` is the workspace that brings the repositories together as git submodules: the
control plane, the console, the CLI, the OpenTofu modules and this site.

985.content: The first run builds two images from the submodules:

986.content: `orkstage/platform:local`, shared by the API, the worker, the console and the `migrate` job.

987.content: `orkstage/tofu-runner:local`, which contains OpenTofu 1.12.7 and the OpenTofu modules.

988.content:
The `migrate` job runs once. It applies the database migrations, loads the demo data and exits. Running
it again is safe: the seed updates existing records instead of duplicating them.

989.content: If you have pnpm installed, `pnpm platform:up` runs the same command.

991.content:
| Service                    | URL                            |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Control API and OpenAPI UI | http://localhost:4000/api/docs |

994.content: Sign in with the **development login**. The seed creates three users:

995.content:
| Email                 | Role                                                              |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `admin@example.local` | Platform owner: full access, including cloud targets and settings |

996.content:
| Email                    | Role                                                       |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `operator@example.local` | Platform operator: deploys, approves and manages incidents |

997.content:
| Email                    | Role                                     |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| `customer@example.local` | Customer owner of the tenant *Acme Corp* |

998.content:
The seed registers simulated AWS, Azure and OCI targets and an instance called **Acme Production**,
built from the `multicloud-reference` template. Its API runs on simulated AWS ECS Fargate behind an
ALB, with ECR and Route 53. Its Postgres database runs on simulated Azure Flexible Server, and its
object storage on simulated OCI.

1000.content:
Open the **Plan & cost** tab. It shows the resolved resources grouped by provider, the policy
results, the links between clouds and the approximate monthly cost.

1001.content:
Click **Deploy**. Acme Production is a `production` instance, so the deployment includes an
approval step. The step is skipped, with a recorded reason, when the plan has no high risk or
destructive changes.

1002.content: Follow the steps and the event log as they update, or open **Deployments** for the timeline.

1003.content:
On a resource of a simulated instance, open **Simulate** and choose **Mark unhealthy**. Within one
health check interval (30 seconds in the compose file), the instance becomes degraded, an incident
opens, an email arrives in Mailpit and the private status page changes. Choose **Mark healthy** and
the incident resolves on its own.

1004.content:
The seed also creates the target **Local AWS (MiniStack)** and the instance **Acme Staging (local
AWS)**, built from `starter-standard`. That instance contains a VPC, ECR, an ALB, RDS Postgres,
Valkey, SQS, two ECS Fargate services, Route 53 and ACM. Deploying it runs OpenTofu for real against
MiniStack. Continue with Local AWS with MiniStack.

1005.content:
For hot reload during development, run only the infrastructure in Docker. Run the apps on the host
with Node.js 24 and pnpm 12, from the `orkstage-dev` checkout:

1011.content: Connect an Azure subscription with a service principal, prepare the Blob state container, and see what OrkStage creates on Container Apps and Flexible Server.

1020.content:
The Azure adapter is covered by unit tests and its OpenTofu modules pass `tofu validate`. It has
not been verified against a live subscription yet.

1021.content:
OrkStage creates Azure resources with OpenTofu (`hashicorp/azurerm` 5.x) in a throwaway runner
container, one isolated state per resource, kept in a Blob container in your own subscription.
Health, secrets, logs and the restart action use the Azure Resource Manager, Key Vault and Log
Analytics REST APIs.

Every resource gets its own resource group (`<name>-rg`), so destroying it removes everything it

1030.content:
Services receive `<ID>_HOST`, `<ID>_PORT`, `<ID>_URL`, `<ID>_BUCKET` and `<ID>_ENDPOINT` for each

identity for storage access.

1031.content:
PostgreSQL passwords are generated with an ephemeral resource and written through write only
attributes, so they never enter OpenTofu state. Module outputs carry only the Key Vault secret id
(`secret_ref`).

1032.content:
Production resources get Key Vault purge protection, a `CanNotDelete` lock on databases and
storage accounts, and resource groups that refuse to be deleted while they still hold resources.

OrkStage signs in with a service principal and a client secret. The secret behind `credentialRef`

`ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID`). Workload identity federation, with no stored secret, is planned.

Owner on the subscription covers the first two. OrkStage gives itself Key Vault Secrets Officer on

Resource providers are registered on first use (`Microsoft.App`, `Microsoft.OperationalInsights`,

1050.content: Logs come from the `ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL` table of the Log Analytics workspace.

1051.content:
Container Apps run on the Consumption profile: up to 4 vCPU and 8 GiB per replica, and memory
is always twice the vCPU, so the size follows the larger of `cpu` and `memoryMiB`.

1052.content: Images must be pullable without credentials. Private registries are not wired yet.

1053.content: The CPU scale rule cannot wake an app from zero, so autoscaled apps keep at least one replica.

1054.content:
PostgreSQL backups cannot be turned off (minimum 7 days). High availability needs the General
Purpose tier, so `micro` and `small` move to `GP_Standard_D2ds_v5` when HA is requested.

1055.content:
Private PostgreSQL needs a network in the same placement slot. With `publicAccess`, the server
accepts connections from Azure services only.

1056.content:
Managed Redis replication is on or off: any `replicas` above zero, or production, turns high
availability on.

1057.content:
Blob Storage has shared keys turned off. Clients use Microsoft Entra identities, so the storage
account hands no keys to resources on other providers.

1058.content:
Credentials published outside Azure Key Vault (another provider's `secret_ref`) reach a
container app only as `<ID>_CREDENTIALS_REF`.

1059.content:
Front Door routes are created before the apps behind them. A route answers once its service has
been deployed and joined its origin group. Only public apps can be origins.

1060.content:
Zone redundancy of the Container Apps environment (`availabilityZones` above 1) needs a region
with availability zones.

1062.content: Connect CoreWeave with an API token, prepare the AI Object Storage state bucket, and run container services with GPUs on an existing CKS cluster.

1074.content:
The CoreWeave adapter is covered by unit tests and its OpenTofu modules pass `tofu validate`. It
has not been verified against a live organization yet.

1075.content:
OrkStage creates VPCs and AI Object Storage buckets with the `coreweave/coreweave` OpenTofu
provider. Container services and ingress routes are Kubernetes objects on an **existing**
CoreWeave Kubernetes Service (CKS) cluster, created with the `hashicorp/kubernetes` provider.
OpenTofu state lives in an AI Object Storage bucket you own.

1076.content:
CoreWeave has no managed PostgreSQL, Redis or queue service. Place those resources on another
provider in the same instance; a CoreWeave service that depends on them receives their
connection settings as environment variables and their credentials as a Kubernetes Secret.

1077.content:
| Template resource | Capability      | What gets created                                                                                                                                |
| ----------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `network`         | `vpc` (default) | `coreweave_networking_vpc` with pod, service and internal load balancer prefixes ready for a CKS cluster. One zone; internet egress is built in. |

1078.content:
| Template resource           | Capability                 | What gets created                                                                                    |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `compute.container-service` | `cks-deployment` (default) | Namespace, Deployment, Service, optional HorizontalPodAutoscaler and Ingress on the target's cluster |

1079.content:
| Template resource | Capability                    | What gets created                                                                        |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `object-storage`  | `ai-object-storage` (default) | `coreweave_object_storage_bucket`, private, with optional versioning and expiration rule |

1080.content:
| Template resource | Capability              | What gets created                                                                                                        |
| ----------------- | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `ingress`         | `cks-ingress` (default) | Host name under the cluster domain, served by the installed controller (CoreWeave Traefik chart) with `cert-manager` TLS |

1081.content: `cpu` and `memoryMiB` become resource requests. Memory is also the limit.

1082.content:
`public: true` creates a `LoadBalancer` Service with the
`service.beta.kubernetes.io/coreweave-load-balancer-type: public` annotation. The module waits
for the public IP and outputs `url`.

1083.content:
`autoscaling` creates a HorizontalPodAutoscaler on CPU. The Deployment then leaves the replica
count to it.

1084.content:
GPUs come from `overrides.coreweave.gpu` in the template. `count` (1 to 8) becomes the
`nvidia.com/gpu` limit; `class` adds required node affinity on the `gpu.nvidia.com/class` node
label. Check the class values on your nodes with `kubectl get nodes -L gpu.nvidia.com/class`.

1085.content:
Each routed service creates an Ingress object for its path in its own namespace, with the ingress
host, the IngressClass and, when `tls` is on, the `cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer` annotation. The
controller merges them under one host. Install the CoreWeave Traefik and `cert-issuer` charts (or set
`ingressClassName`, `clusterIssuer` and `ingressDomain` for your own controller) before deploying.

1086.content:
Connection settings of dependencies (`<ID>_HOST`, `<ID>_PORT`, `<ID>_URL`, `<ID>_BUCKET`,
`<ID>_ENDPOINT`) are plain environment variables. Credentials published through `secret_ref`, for
example a PostgreSQL password on AWS or Supabase, are read from the owning provider at deploy time
and stored in the Kubernetes Secret `<name>-deps`, loaded with `envFrom` as `<ID>_PASSWORD`,
`<ID>_USERNAME`, `<ID>_URL` and so on. They pass to OpenTofu as the sensitive `TF_VAR_secret_env`
and are kept in the OpenTofu state, like any Kubernetes Secret managed by OpenTofu.

1087.content:
| `config` field | Required | Meaning                                                                   |
| -------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `stateBucket`  | yes      | AI Object Storage bucket for OpenTofu state. Must exist before deploying. |

1088.content:
| `config` field | Required                 | Meaning                                         |
| -------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `clusterName`  | for services and ingress | Existing CKS cluster that workloads deploy into |

| `config` field | Required | Meaning                                                                                                 |
| -------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `zone`         | no       | Zone of the cluster and the state bucket, for example `US-EAST-04A`. Defaults to the deployment region. |

| `stateEndpoint` | no       | S3 endpoint for state. Defaults to `https://cwobject.com`. |

1091.content:
| `config` field     | Required | Meaning                                                 |
| ------------------ | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ingressClassName` | no       | IngressClass for ingress routes. Defaults to `traefik`. |

1092.content:
| `config` field  | Required | Meaning                                                                      |
| --------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `clusterIssuer` | no       | `cert-manager` ClusterIssuer for TLS routes. Defaults to `letsencrypt-prod`. |

| --------------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ingressDomain` | no       | DNS suffix served by the ingress controller. Defaults to `<organization id>-<clusterName>.coreweave.app`. |

1094.content:
`token`: a CoreWeave API access token (Console, Tokens). The OpenTofu runner receives it as
`COREWEAVE_API_TOKEN`. CKS managed auth accepts the same token as a Kubernetes bearer token, so
with `clusterName` set no kubeconfig is needed: the adapter looks up the cluster's API server
endpoint through the CKS API.

1095.content:
`stateAccessKeyId` and `stateSecretAccessKey`: an AI Object Storage access key that can read and
write the state bucket and the buckets OrkStage creates.

1096.content:
`kubeconfig`: only for clusters reached another way (a private endpoint, a different token).
The current context's server, `certificate-authority-data` and bearer `token` are used. Client
certificates and exec plugins are not supported.

1097.content:
Cluster access reaches OpenTofu as `TF_VAR_k8s_host`, `TF_VAR_k8s_token` and `TF_VAR_k8s_ca` for
one command. Nothing is written to disk and no secret is part of the configuration.

1098.content:
AI Object Storage is S3 compatible and accepts only virtual hosted style requests
(`https://<bucket>.cwobject.com`). Before the first deployment:

1099.content:
As an organization admin, create an organization access policy that lets the principal behind
the access key use AI Object Storage (Console, Object Storage, Policies). Without a policy every
S3 request is denied.

1100.content: Create an access key (Console, Object Storage, Keys) and put it in the credential secret.

1102.content:
The S3 backend runs without native locking, because conditional writes are not confirmed for AI
Object Storage. OrkStage already runs one operation per resource at a time.

1103.content:
API token: read the caller identity, list CKS clusters, create and delete VPCs, create and
delete AI Object Storage buckets and their versioning and lifecycle settings.

1105.content:
AI Object Storage access key: read and write the state bucket; read the buckets OrkStage creates
(health checks).

1106.content:
`allowedRegions` and `defaultRegion` are CoreWeave zone names such as `US-EAST-04A`. VPCs and
buckets are created in the deployment region. A VPC lives in one zone.

1107.content:
| Capability       | Action    | Parameters | Effect                                                                                                              |
| ---------------- | --------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `cks-deployment` | `restart` | none       | Rolling restart of every pod of the Deployment, like `kubectl rollout restart`, keeping the same image and settings |

1108.content: Logs are the last lines of up to three pods.

1109.content:
OrkStage does not create CKS clusters or node pools. Workloads go to the cluster in
`clusterName` (or the kubeconfig). The `vpc` capability is not attached to that cluster.

1110.content: Images must be pullable by the cluster nodes. Registry pull secrets are not managed.

1111.content:
AI Object Storage access keys are scoped to a principal, not a bucket, so buckets publish no
`secret_ref` and other providers cannot be handed credentials for them.

1112.content:
Buckets have no force destroy: empty a bucket before deleting it. The template `tier` and
`publicAccess` are not applied.

1113.content:
Several routed services request their own certificate for the same host (one per namespace).
Mind the Let's Encrypt duplicate certificate limit.

1114.content: GPU hours are billed per node and are not part of the cost estimate.

1116.content: Connect a DigitalOcean team with an API token and Spaces keys, prepare the state bucket, and see what OrkStage creates on App Platform and managed databases.

It has not been verified against a live team yet.

`orkstage-modules/modules/digitalocean`, one isolated state per resource, kept in a Spaces bucket

1134.content:
Database credentials are never module outputs. PostgreSQL and Valkey publish
`secret_ref = do-db://<cluster id>`, and the adapter reads the connection details from the
DigitalOcean API (`readSecret`) when a resource on another provider needs them. App Platform
services receive `<ID>_URL` for each DigitalOcean database they depend on as a `SECRET` variable.

1135.content:
| `config` field | Required | Example                 | Meaning                                   |
| -------------- | -------- | ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `stateBucket`  | yes      | `acme-orkstage-tfstate` | Existing Spaces bucket for OpenTofu state |

1136.content:
| `config` field | Required | Example | Meaning                      |
| -------------- | -------- | ------- | ---------------------------- |
| `stateRegion`  | yes      | `nyc3`  | Spaces region of that bucket |

1137.content:
The values reach OpenTofu only as runner environment variables (`DIGITALOCEAN_TOKEN`,
`SPACES_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `SPACES_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, and `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and
`AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` for the state backend).

1138.content: Create the bucket once, before validating the target. OrkStage never creates it.

1139.content:
The backend signs as `us-east-1` against `https://<stateRegion>.digitaloceanspaces.com`, as
DigitalOcean documents, and locks state with `use_lockfile`.

1140.content:
A full access token works. A custom scoped token needs create, read, update and delete on `vpc`,
`app` and `database`, plus `account:read` and `tag:create`. Validation probes the VPC, App
Platform and database scopes and fails when a scope needed by the resources about to be deployed
is missing.

1142.content:
App Platform joins a VPC only from one datacenter per region: `ams3`, `atl1`, `blr1`, `fra1`,
`lon1`, `nyc1`, `sfo3`, `sgp1`, `syd1`, `tor1`. In other regions (for example `nyc3`) a service
cannot reach a private database, and deploying such a pair fails validation. Use one of those
regions or give the database public access. Spaces is not offered in `nyc1`.

1143.content:
| Capability     | Action     | Parameters                             | Effect                                                                   |
| -------------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `app-platform` | `redeploy` | `forceBuild` (boolean, default `true`) | New App Platform deployment of the current spec, pulling the image again |

1144.content:
| Capability     | Action    | Parameters | Effect                                                            |
| -------------- | --------- | ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `app-platform` | `restart` | none       | Rolling restart of the service instances without a new deployment |

1145.content: Deployment history and run logs come from the App Platform API.

1146.content:
App Platform pulls images from DigitalOcean Container Registry, Docker Hub and GHCR only.
Private Docker Hub or GHCR images need registry credentials, which are not wired yet.

1147.content: Autoscaling needs a dedicated CPU instance size. Shared sizes run a fixed instance count.

1148.content:
Credentials of dependencies on other providers reach the service as `<ID>_CREDENTIALS_REF`
references, not values.

1149.content: Services do not receive Spaces keys for their buckets, only the bucket name and endpoint.

1150.content: Managed database backups are daily with 7 days of recovery. Retention is not configurable.

1151.content:
From 15 October 2026 (new accounts) and 30 November 2026 (all accounts), new Standard Edition
PostgreSQL clusters cannot add standby nodes or use plans above 4 GiB. Use
`overrides.digitalocean.size` with an Advanced Edition slug when you need them.

1152.content: A VPC spans the datacenter, so availability zones and NAT gateways are not modelled.

1153.content: There is no load balancer capability yet. `ingress` is App Platform routing only.

1154.content:
Production resources keep `force_destroy` off on buckets. DigitalOcean has no deletion protection
flag for database clusters.

1173.content:
Cloud Run services mount database and cache credentials from Secret Manager as
`<ID>_CREDENTIALS`, and get read and write access to the buckets they depend on.

1174.content:
The PostgreSQL app password lives in OpenTofu state and in a Secret Manager secret
(`secret_ref`). The Redis AUTH string is stored in Secret Manager too. `readSecret` returns
`username`, `password`, `host`, `port`, `database` and `url` for PostgreSQL, and `password`,
`host`, `port` and `url` for Redis, so a resource on another provider can connect.

The secret behind `credentialRef` is the service account key JSON file exactly as Google issues
it. The adapter needs `client_email` and `private_key`, and also reads `private_key_id` and
`project_id` when present.

1178.content:
The key signs a short JWT that is exchanged for an OAuth access token, cached in memory. It
reaches OpenTofu only as the `GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS` environment variable of one runner command.
Workload identity federation, with no long lived key, is planned.

1179.content: Create the bucket once, in the region you deploy to most:

1180.content:

configuration applied is kept beside it as `orkstage/<name>.tfstate.config.json`, so destroy never
depends on a newer template.

Regions are Google Cloud regions such as `us-central1`, `southamerica-east1` or `europe-west1`.
Subnets span every zone of a region, so `availabilityZones` does not change the network layout.

1196.content:
Cloud Run CPU is rounded up to 1, 2, 4, 6 or 8 vCPU, and memory is raised to the minimum for
that CPU. Fractional CPU would force one request per instance.

1197.content: Cloud Run scales on request concurrency. `targetCpuPercent` is not used.

1198.content:
There is no shared HTTPS load balancer with path routing yet. Each service keeps its own
`run.app` URL.

1199.content: Same zone HA is not offered for Cloud SQL; regional availability is the HA option.

1200.content:
A PostgreSQL instance without a network gets a public IP with no authorized networks, reachable
only through Cloud SQL connectors.

1201.content:
Memorystore needs a network in the same slot and runs without in transit encryption; traffic
stays inside the VPC. Two or more replicas need at least 5 GB, so small sizes are raised.

1202.content: The private services peering is abandoned on destroy and removed with the network.

1203.content: Credentials of dependencies outside Google Cloud are not mounted into Cloud Run.

1205.content: The clouds and platforms OrkStage deploys to, what each one offers for every resource type, how credentials work and where OpenTofu state lives.

1213.content:
A template names resource types such as `database.postgresql` or `web.frontend`, never a provider.
When you create an instance, each placement slot is bound to a **cloud target** (one account,
project, team or workspace of a provider) and a region. The provider adapter behind that target
turns each resource into real infrastructure.

1214.content:
AWS is tested against MiniStack and runs on real accounts. The other adapters on this page are in
Preview: they are covered by unit tests, and the OpenTofu modules of the
infrastructure clouds pass `tofu validate`, but none of them has been verified against a live
account yet. Expect changes. Preview providers are **disabled by default**; see
enabling a provider.

1215.content:
**Infrastructure clouds** (AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure,
DigitalOcean, Vultr, CoreWeave and Magalu Cloud) are deployed with **OpenTofu**. For each resource,
the worker runs an OpenTofu module in a throwaway runner container. Every resource has its own
state file, kept in a bucket or container **in your own account**. OrkStage keeps outputs and
references, not the state.

1216.content:
**Application platforms** (Vercel, Render and Supabase) are driven through their **REST APIs**.
There is no OpenTofu, no module and no state store: the platform itself holds the state, and the
adapter finds its resources again by name, so repeating a deployment converges the existing
resource instead of creating a second one.

1217.content: Both kinds can be mixed in one instance. See mixing providers.

1218.content:
Each cell is the capability id you can set in a resource's `implementation` field. When a type has
more than one capability, the first one is the default. "Not offered" means the provider has no
capability for that type: place that resource on another provider.
