2014.content:
The overview shows instance and deployment counts, health, open incidents and trends. On a new
installation it also shows an **onboarding checklist**:

2015.content: Connect or validate a cloud target.

2020.content:
The instance list shows the status, health, environment, template version and tenant of each
instance. An instance page has five tabs:

2021.content:
| Tab      | What it shows                                                                                |
| -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Overview | Details, variables, the topology diagram, resources with their placement, outputs and health |

2022.content:
| Tab         | What it shows                                                                           |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Plan & cost | A fresh preview: resolved resources, policies, connectivity, cost estimate and the diff |

2023.content:
| Tab         | What it shows                                               |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Deployments | Every deployment of this instance, with status and duration |

2024.content:
| Tab  | What it shows                                                               |
| ---- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Logs | Recent log lines per resource (CloudWatch Logs on AWS, simulated elsewhere) |

2025.content:
| Tab     | What it shows                                          |
| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Metrics | CPU, memory, requests, latency and errors per resource |

2026.content:
The page header holds three actions: **Deploy**, **Upgrade template** and **Destroy**. Each one
appears only when your role allows it.

2027.content:
**Deployments** lists every deployment across the instances you can see. A deployment page shows
the step list, a Gantt timeline, the plan and the event log. When they apply, it also shows
**Approve**, **Cancel** and **Retry**.

2028.content: **Incidents** lists open and resolved incidents with their updates.

2029.content:
The console uses the dark theme by default. Switch to the light theme from the user menu. The
console applies your choice before the first paint, so the page never flashes the wrong theme.

2031.content: Create an OrkStage instance with the six step wizard. Pick the tenant and template, bind each slot to a target and region, then set variables.

2039.content: Doing the same through the API

2040.content:
A new instance starts as a `DRAFT`, and nothing is provisioned until you
deploy it. Open **Instances**, then **New instance**. Creating an
instance needs a platform owner or admin role, or the customer owner or admin role in the tenant.

2041.content:
Choose the customer that owns the instance. The tenant's plan decides which templates and
placements are allowed, and the instance's cost is attributed to that tenant.

2042.content:
Pick a template and one of its **published** versions. Published versions never change, and drafts
cannot be used. Templates marked `nonProduction` show a warning. The `non-production-template`
policy fails if you use one for a `production` instance.

2043.content:
| Predefined template | Profile                         | Plans         |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------- |
| `free-validation`   | `shared-sandbox`, nonproduction | FREE, SANDBOX |

2044.content:
| Predefined template | Profile                            | Plans            |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| `sandbox-min-cost`  | `dedicated-sandbox`, nonproduction | SANDBOX, STARTER |

2045.content:
| Predefined template | Profile   | Plans           |
| ------------------- | --------- | --------------- |
| `starter-standard`  | `starter` | STARTER, GROWTH |

2046.content:
| Predefined template | Profile  | Plans         |
| ------------------- | -------- | ------------- |
| `growth-standard`   | `growth` | GROWTH, SCALE |

2048.content:
| Predefined template    | Profile  | Plans         |
| ---------------------- | -------- | ------------- |
| `multicloud-reference` | `growth` | GROWTH, SCALE |

2049.content:
Bind every **placement slot** of the template to a **cloud target** and a **region**. Slots can
use different clouds. With `multicloud-reference`, for example, `primary` can run on AWS, `data` on
Azure and `storage` on OCI. The list offers only targets whose provider the slot accepts, and only
the regions each target allows.

2050.content:
Simulated targets (the mock provider) carry a simulated label. Use them to rehearse a topology
before you connect real accounts.

2051.content:
Templates expose a few typed variables, for example `apiReplicas` or `databaseSize`. The form
starts with the default values. The browser checks ranges and allowed values, and the API checks
them again.

2052.content:
Give the instance a name and a slug. The slug is lowercase and goes into physical resource names
such as `ork-acme-staging-api`. Then choose the environment: `production`, `staging`, `development`
or `sandbox`. Production instances get stricter policies (backups are required) and an approval
step for high risk changes.

2053.content:
Check the summary and create the draft. The console opens the instance page, where the
Plan & cost tab previews what a deployment would do.

2054.content: The API key needs the `instances:write` scope. See API keys.

2056.content: Start an OrkStage deployment and follow it live. Approve high risk production changes, cancel, retry failed resources, upgrade and destroy safely.

2063.content:
Click **Deploy** on an instance. The API validates the request, records the deployment with all its
steps and answers at once with `202`. The worker then does the work, so you can close the browser.

2064.content:
| Phase                          | What happens                                                                      |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Validate template and policies | The stored snapshot is checked again. A failing policy stops the deployment here. |

2065.content:
| Phase                  | What happens                                                                                           |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Validate cloud targets | Checks credentials, the state bucket and, on real AWS, the IAM permissions the deployed services need. |

2066.content:
| Phase         | What happens                                                                               |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Generate plan | Builds the platform diff, plus a real `tofu plan` for each existing resource that changes. |

2067.content:
| Phase    | What happens                                                                                      |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Approval | Runs only for high risk production changes (see below). Otherwise it is skipped, with the reason. |

2068.content:
| Phase     | What happens                                                                      |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Resources | One step per resource, in dependency order. Independent branches run in parallel. |

2069.content:
| Phase                                      | What happens                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Remove resources no longer in the template | Deletes resources the instance still has but the template no longer contains (after an upgrade, or a resource turned off by a variable), dependents first. The plan lists them as deletions, so production approval covers them. A destroy protected instance keeps them, with a warning. |

2070.content:
| Phase               | What happens                                                                      |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Application rollout | Services run their images by digest, so the exact image never changes under them. |

2071.content:
| Phase                             | What happens                                                         |
| --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Configure secrets and connections | Wires connection references. Secret values stay in the secret store. |

2072.content:
| Phase                                | What happens                                                        |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Health and connectivity verification | Checks each resource until it is healthy, within one settle window. |

2073.content:
| Phase                            | What happens                                                          |
| -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Register observability, Finalize | Registers monitoring and moves the instance to `READY` or `DEGRADED`. |

2074.content:
The deployment page shows each step with its status, the Gantt **timeline** and the **event log**.
It refreshes every 1.5 seconds while the deployment runs.

2075.content:
A deployment of a `production` instance stops at `AWAITING_APPROVAL` when the change is high risk.
That happens in two cases:

2076.content: The platform plan deletes or replaces a resource, or changes an existing database.

2077.content:
The **provider plan** deletes or replaces something. This is a real `tofu plan`, run for each
changed resource during the plan phase. It can find a replacement even when the platform diff
shows only an update, for example when an attribute forces replacement. Routine ECS task
definition revisions do not count.

2078.content:
The event log shows the provider plan for every changed resource, and destructive ones appear as
warnings:

2079.content:
OrkStage notifies the owners and admins, and the `deployment.awaiting_approval` webhook fires. A
user with the `approve` permission clicks **Approve**, and the deployment continues.

2080.content:
When the plan contains no high risk change, the approval step is marked skipped with the reason
`Not needed: no high-risk or destructive changes planned.` Instances in other environments
(`staging`, `development`, `sandbox`) never wait for approval.

2081.content:
Transient failures, such as throttling and timeouts, are retried with exponential backoff.
Destructive operations are never retried automatically.

2082.content:
A failed resource skips only the resources that depend on it, and unrelated branches finish.
Partial failure is a normal outcome, shown per resource. In this example the database fails, so
the API that depends on it is skipped, while storage and the cache finish:

2083.content:
**Retry** runs only the failed and skipped resources again. Resources that already converged are
left alone.

2084.content:
**Cancel** stops the deployment cooperatively. The worker checks for the request while it runs,
and resources that have not started yet are marked cancelled.

2085.content:
If the worker restarts, the deployment resumes. Finished phases are skipped, and converged
resources (same idempotency key) are not applied again.

2086.content:
Someone may delete a resource directly in the provider console. During verification, OrkStage asks
the provider whether each resource still exists. A missing resource fails verification at once,
with the message `Resource no longer exists at the provider. Redeploy to re-create it.`, instead of
waiting for it to settle. The next deployment creates it again.

2087.content:
**Change template version** shows the plan from what runs now to the chosen version (what is
created, updated and deleted), then starts a deployment of that version. The instance keeps its
current version until that deployment succeeds, so a failed upgrade leaves it on the version that
actually runs; **Retry** continues the upgrade. Choosing an older version rolls back the same way.
Production upgrades that delete or replace resources wait for approval. An instance never changes
version on its own.

2088.content:
Through the API: `POST /instances/{id}/preview?templateVersionId={version}` returns the plan, and
`POST /instances/{id}/upgrade` with `{ "templateVersionId": "..." }` starts the deployment.

2089.content: **Destroy** removes every cloud resource in reverse dependency order:

2090.content:
To confirm, you type the instance slug. An instance marked *Destroy protected* refuses to be
destroyed. Only customer owners and admins, and platform owners and admins, can destroy an
instance. Destroying a `production` instance also waits for an approval before anything is
deleted; cancelling it at that point leaves the instance `READY`.

2091.content:
The backup phase checks that a backup policy exists. It does not yet verify that a backup can be
restored.

2093.content: Turn Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes or Docker Compose files into a draft OrkStage template, review the evidence and create the template.

2097.content:
**Templates**, then **Import**, turns existing infrastructure code into a draft template. The
OrkStage scan engine detects and maps the resources. It is the same engine the `ork` CLI uses.

2098.content:
Choose a folder or individual files. The console keeps only the text files the engine understands,
such as `.tf`, `.tf.json`, YAML, JSON, TOML, `Dockerfile`, `package.json`, `go.mod`,
`requirements.txt` and `Chart.yaml`. It skips the `node_modules`, `.git`, `.terraform`, `.next`,
`target`, `vendor`, `dist` and `build` folders. Each file can be at most 512 KiB, and the upload at
most 5 MB in total. The server scans the files with the engine compiled to WebAssembly
(`@orkstage/scan`).

2099.content:
If the server answers `501 SCANNER_UNAVAILABLE`, scanning is not installed on that server. Scan
locally with the CLI instead.

2100.content: `ork import` scans on your machine, sends only the report, and prints a console link:

2101.content: Open the link and the page loads that import directly. The CLI is in Preview.

2102.content: The import page shows five things:

2103.content:
**Resources**: each detected resource with its OrkStage type, provider, implementation,
confidence (`high`, `medium` or `low`) and the source evidence, such as
`main.tf:12 aws_db_instance.main`.

2104.content:
**Connections** inferred from references, for example a task definition that reads the database
address.

2105.content: **Unmapped** items: what the engine saw but cannot express in a template, with the reason.

2106.content: **Warnings** and the **validation** result of the generated template.

2108.content:
Give the template a name and a display name, then click **Create draft and open builder**.
OrkStage creates a `DRAFT` template at version `0.1.0` and opens it in the builder. Fix what the
validation reported, then publish it.

2109.content:
Each import produces at most one template. Only platform owners and admins can create templates.
Other users see a note asking them to share the import id with a platform admin.

2110.content: See Importing IaC for supported sources, mapping rules and the API.

2112.content: Browse curated and community templates with review badges, see their resources and cost before you deploy, and submit your own templates for review.

2119.content:
The marketplace lists templates ready to deploy: complete architectures such as disaster recovery,
a payment gateway, an ecommerce storefront, logistics tracking or last mile delivery. Every
listing is a normal OrkStage template, so it goes through the same placement, plan, policy and
approval checks as any other before anything is created.

2120.content:
| Badge        | Meaning                                                           |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Verified** | Reviewed by platform staff: policies, security defaults and cost. |

2121.content:
| Badge               | Meaning                                                                           |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **DevOps reviewed** | Reviewed for operations: backups, health checks, observability and safe defaults. |

2122.content:
Badges are given by reviewers (platform admins and owners) when they approve a listing. A listing
loses its badges when its author edits it, until it is reviewed again. The curated listings that
ship with OrkStage carry both badges.

2123.content:
Open **Marketplace** in the console. Search by name, summary or tag, and filter by category,
provider or badge; sort by use, date or name. Each card shows the providers the template can run
on, an approximate monthly cost and how often it was starred and used.

2124.content:
A listing page shows the description, every resource with its estimated monthly cost, the
placement slots and the providers each one allows, the plans it fits, its triggers and the full
template source.

2125.content:
The cost is computed on the first provider each placement slot allows, in a representative
region, at static list prices. Your own targets, regions and variables change it. The plan review
before each deployment shows the estimate for your actual choices.

2126.content:
**Use this template** opens the instance wizard with the template and its published version
already selected; you choose the tenant, bind each placement slot to your cloud targets and set
the variables. Templates that need more than one provider require a plan with multiple
providers (GROWTH or SCALE).

2127.content:
**Clone and customize** (template authors) copies the template so you can change it in the
builder and publish your own version.

2128.content: **Star** keeps a listing in mind and helps others find popular ones.

2129.content:
Template authors (the `publish` permission on templates) can submit a template that has a
published version: **Marketplace > Submit a template**, then a slug, title, summary, description,
one to four categories and optional tags. The listing stays hidden until it is reviewed; your
submissions and their review notes are under **My submissions**.

2130.content:
Reviewers see the queue under **Review queue** and approve (with badges), reject or later unlist a
listing. Every submission, edit and review is recorded in the audit log.

2131.content:
The same operations are available under `/api/v1/marketplace/listings` (see the
API reference). Browsing and `use` accept API keys with the
`templates:read` scope; submitting and reviewing need a signed in user.

2132.content:
The `TEMPLATE_MARKETPLACE` feature flag (on by default) hides the marketplace for the whole
platform; see enabling a provider for how flags are
changed.

2134.content: Who OrkStage notifies about deployments and incidents, through which channels (the console, email, signed webhooks), and what is not available yet.

2139.content:
| Channel                                 | Status    |
| --------------------------------------- | --------- |
| In the console (the bell in the header) | Available |

2140.content:
| Channel                         | Status    |
| ------------------------------- | --------- |
| Email (SMTP, through an outbox) | Available |

2141.content:
| Channel                               | Status    |
| ------------------------------------- | --------- |
| Webhooks (HTTP POST signed with HMAC) | Available |

2142.content:
| Channel                | Status  |
| ---------------------- | ------- |
| Slack, Microsoft Teams | Planned |

2143.content:
Notifications go to the tenant's **owners and admins** and to **platform owners and admins**.
Examples:

2144.content: a deployment started, succeeded or failed;

2145.content: a production deployment is waiting for approval;

2146.content: an instance became degraded, or drift was detected on one of its resources;

2147.content: an incident was opened, updated or resolved.

2148.content:
Each notification in the console links to its deployment, instance or incident. Mark it as read from
the bell. The matching API routes are `GET /notifications` and `POST /notifications/:id/read`.

2149.content:
The worker queues emails in an outbox and sends them through SMTP (`SMTP_HOST`, `SMTP_PORT`,
`SMTP_SECURE`, `EMAIL_FROM`). It retries a failed email later, up to 5 attempts in total. In the
local stack, emails land in Mailpit at http://localhost:8025.

2150.content:
Notification preferences per user. The data model stores them, but no screen or API sets them
yet.

2151.content: Slack and Teams channels. Until then, point a webhook at a receiver that forwards to them.

2153.content: Inspect a running OrkStage instance. The topology diagram with placement and health, drift, resource outputs, recent logs and metrics per resource.

2160.content:
The **Overview** tab of an instance draws its topology. Every resource is a node, grouped by
provider, target and region. Dependency edges connect the nodes, and connectivity links carry the
strategy label, for example `public-tls-allowlist` between AWS and Azure. Node colors follow
health, and simulated resources carry a *simulated* label.

2161.content:
**Copy as Mermaid** copies the same diagram as a Mermaid flowchart, ready for a design document or
a pull request description.

2162.content:
Below the diagram, the resource table shows each resource's type, capability, physical name, target
and region, knowledge state (`DESIRED`, `KNOWN`, `ACTUAL` or `UNKNOWN`), drift and health.

2163.content:
On real providers, the worker runs a scheduled **drift scan**. It runs every
`DRIFT_CHECK_INTERVAL_MINUTES` minutes (default 360), and `0` turns it off. The scan plans each
applied resource again with OpenTofu, from the snapshot it was deployed with. If that plan contains
any change, something changed outside OrkStage.

2164.content:
When that happens, OrkStage marks the resource `DRIFT_DETECTED` with the planned actions, writes an
audit event and notifies owners and admins (`instance.drift_detected`). Resources with a pending
change are skipped, because that change is a deployment, not drift. **Deploy** restores the
template's configuration.

2165.content: On simulated targets, drift is checked on every health check instead.

2166.content:
Each provisioned resource exposes the outputs its module produced, for example the database `host`
and `port`, the ingress `url`, the queue `queue_url` or the bucket `endpoint`. Secrets are never
outputs. The database password lives in AWS Secrets Manager, and services receive its ARN.

2167.content:
The **Logs** tab shows recent log lines for a resource
(`GET /instances/:id/logs?resourceId=&limit=`). On AWS they come from the service's CloudWatch log
group. On simulated targets they are generated.

2168.content:
The **Metrics** tab charts CPU, memory, requests per minute, p95 latency and errors per minute for
the last hour (`GET /instances/:id/metrics?resourceId=&metric=cpu&minutes=60`).

2169.content:
Metrics for real AWS resources (CloudWatch `GetMetricData`) and traces are on the roadmap. The
charts are filled only for simulated targets.

2170.content:
On simulated targets, users who can deploy or update the instance see **Simulation controls**:
**Mark unhealthy**, **Mark degraded**, **Mark healthy**, **Clear health override** and **Introduce
drift** (or **Clear drift**). They drive the loop from health to incident to notification without
breaking anything real.

2172.content: Read an OrkStage plan before you deploy. Placement per provider, policy results, connectivity across clouds, monthly cost, the diff and its risk.

2178.content:
The **Plan & cost** tab of an instance runs a preview (`POST /instances/:id/preview`). The preview
compiles the template with the instance's variables and placements, then compares the result with
what OrkStage already knows about the instance. It never touches a cloud and saves nothing.

2179.content:
The preview lists every resource with the target, region and concrete capability it resolved to,
for example `database → Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server (eastus)`. When a capability
is not available in a region, the preview fails and suggests alternatives.

2180.content: Every policy reports a result, so you see everything that was checked, not only what failed:

2181.content:
| Policy               | Checks                                |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `no-public-database` | No database has `publicAccess: true`. |

2182.content:
| Policy              | Checks                               |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `no-public-storage` | Object storage blocks public access. |

2183.content:
| Policy               | Checks                                     |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `production-backups` | Production databases have backups enabled. |

2184.content:
| Policy                    | Checks                                                                               |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `non-production-template` | Sandbox templates are not used for production. For other environments it only warns. |

2185.content:
| Policy                | Checks                                               |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `encryption-required` | Every chosen capability supports encryption at rest. |

2186.content:
| Policy            | Checks                                              |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `allowed-regions` | The target and the platform both allow each region. |

2187.content:
| Policy         | Checks                                                                |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `max-replicas` | Replica counts stay under the platform limit, when one is configured. |

2188.content:
| Policy             | Checks                                                               |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `max-monthly-cost` | The estimate stays under the monthly budget, when one is configured. |

2189.content:
| Policy                    | Checks                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `multi-cloud-entitlement` | The tenant's plan allows several clouds, or several regions of one provider, when the placements use them. |

2190.content:
| Policy                     | Checks                                                                 |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `cross-cloud-connectivity` | Links between clouds can be satisfied. Warns about latency and egress. |

2191.content: A `fail` result blocks the deployment. Custom templates go through the same policies.

2192.content: For each connectivity requirement in the template, the compiler chooses a strategy:

2193.content:
| Strategy          | When                                              |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `private-network` | Both resources are in the same target and region. |

2194.content:
| Strategy          | When                                                                      |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `private-peering` | Same provider, different account or region. Peering cost and setup apply. |

2195.content:
| Strategy     | When                                                                                     |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `public-tls` | The requirement's mode is `secure`: TLS over the provider network or the public network. |

2196.content:
| Strategy               | When                                                                                              |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `public-tls-allowlist` | Across clouds with `private-preferred`: TLS on a public endpoint that allows only listed sources. |

2197.content:
| Strategy        | When                                                                     |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `unsatisfiable` | Across clouds with `private-required`. Change the mode or the placement. |

2198.content:
OrkStage never creates VPNs or interconnects without telling you. Links between clouds add latency
and may incur egress charges, and the preview says so.

2199.content:
The strategy is chosen and shown, but allowlist rules across clouds are not provisioned yet. One
example is an Azure Postgres firewall rule for AWS NAT addresses.

2200.content:
The estimate uses static list prices from each capability catalog (on demand, monthly, in USD). It
is always labeled **approximate** and is not an invoice. Its confidence is `approximate` when every
resource has a price, `partial` when some do not, and `unavailable` when none do. Lines are grouped
by category: compute, database, cache, storage, network and messaging.

2201.content:
The diff against known resources lists each resource as `CREATE`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `NOOP`,
grouped by provider, target and region. A change of target, region or capability counts as a
replacement. Approval requests and logs use the same plan in plain text:

2202.content:
| Risk   | When                                                              |
| ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `high` | Anything is deleted or replaced, or an existing database changes. |

2203.content:
| Risk     | When                            |
| -------- | ------------------------------- |
| `medium` | Existing resources are updated. |

2204.content:
| Risk  | When                                                 |
| ----- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `low` | The plan only creates resources, or changes nothing. |

2205.content:
The preview shows the platform's view. During the deployment, the worker also runs the real
provider plan for each resource that changes. See Deploying.

2207.content: The seven predefined OrkStage roles (three for the platform, four per tenant), what each can do, and how every request enforces tenant isolation.

2213.content:
OrkStage has seven predefined roles. **Platform roles** apply to the whole installation. **Tenant
roles** apply per tenant, so one user can be an admin in one tenant and a viewer in another.

2214.content:
| Role            | Can                                    |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `PlatformOwner` | Everything, including global settings. |

2215.content:
| Role            | Can                                                                                                                                        |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `PlatformAdmin` | Everything except changing global settings (it can read them) and deleting the organization. Manages cloud targets, templates and tenants. |

2216.content:
| Role               | Can                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `PlatformOperator` | Read everything except settings. Deploy, restart, scale and approve instances. Create and update incidents, and update status pages. Cannot manage cloud targets, publish templates or destroy instances. |

2217.content:
| Capability                                                                   | Owner | Admin | Developer | Viewer |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- | ----- | --------- | ------ |
| Read instances, deployments, services, incidents, status page, notifications | ✓     | ✓     | ✓         | ✓      |

2218.content:
| Capability                          | Owner | Admin | Developer | Viewer |
| ----------------------------------- | ----- | ----- | --------- | ------ |
| Read templates, plans, applications | ✓     | ✓     | ✓         | ✓      |

2219.content:
| Capability                   | Owner | Admin | Developer | Viewer |
| ---------------------------- | ----- | ----- | --------- | ------ |
| Deploy and restart instances | ✓     | ✓     | ✓         |        |

2220.content:
| Capability | Owner | Admin | Developer | Viewer |
| ---------- | ----- | ----- | --------- | ------ |
| Import IaC | ✓     | ✓     | ✓         |        |

2221.content:
| Capability                                           | Owner | Admin | Developer | Viewer |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ----- | ----- | --------- | ------ |
| Create, update, scale, destroy and approve instances | ✓     | ✓     |           |        |

2222.content:
| Capability                                     | Owner | Admin | Developer | Viewer |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ----- | ----- | --------- | ------ |
| See the team (members and pending invitations) | ✓     | ✓     | ✓         | ✓      |

2223.content:
| Capability         | Owner | Admin | Developer | Viewer |
| ------------------ | ----- | ----- | --------- | ------ |
| Read the audit log | ✓     | ✓     |           |        |

2224.content:
| Capability                   | Owner | Admin | Developer | Viewer |
| ---------------------------- | ----- | ----- | --------- | ------ |
| Manage API keys and webhooks | ✓     | ✓     |           |        |

2225.content:
| Capability                                                     | Owner | Admin | Developer | Viewer |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- | ----- | --------- | ------ |
| Invite people, change roles, remove members, update the tenant | ✓     |       |           |        |

2226.content: Tenant roles never get access to cloud targets, settings or template publishing.

2227.content:
**Settings > Team** lists the members of a tenant with their roles, and the invitations still
pending. Owners (and platform staff) invite people by email with a role:

2228.content:
The person receives an email with a link that works once and expires after 7 days. The inviter
also sees the link once, to share it directly if the email does not arrive.

2229.content:
They accept it signed in with the invited address; another account is refused. If they sign in
through SSO for the first time with that address, the account is created with the invitation's
membership.

2230.content: Inviting the same address again replaces the previous link. Owners can revoke an invitation.

2231.content:
Owners change roles and remove members; anyone can leave a tenant. A tenant always keeps at least
one owner, so the last owner cannot be demoted or removed until someone else is an owner. Every
invitation, acceptance, role change and removal is in the audit log.

2233.content: The request is authenticated with a session cookie or an API key.

2234.content: Queries for records that belong to a tenant are filtered by the caller's memberships.

2235.content: Every loaded record is checked against the same rules (CASL) before any action.

2236.content: The action is written to the audit log.

2237.content:
A request for another tenant's record gets **404**, not 403, so the response does not reveal that
the record exists. The console receives the rules from `GET /me` only to hide what you cannot do.
The API remains the authority.

2238.content:
An API key acts **with a role**. A tenant key uses `CustomerAdmin`, `CustomerDeveloper` or
`CustomerViewer`. A key for the whole organization uses `PlatformAdmin` or `PlatformOperator`.
Scopes then narrow what the role allows, so a key can never do more than its role.

2239.content:
Custom roles and finer permissions are planned for the Enterprise edition. See
Community vs Enterprise.

2241.content: How OrkStage derives instance health, shows it on a private status page per tenant, opens incidents automatically and lets staff post incident updates.

2242.content: From resource health to instance health

2247.content:
The worker's health monitor checks every active resource through its provider adapter at a fixed
interval: `HEALTH_CHECK_INTERVAL_SECONDS`, 30 by default. Instance health then follows from the
health of its components:

2249.content:
| Components                                 | Instance   |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---------- |
| Any component is `UNHEALTHY` or `DEGRADED` | `DEGRADED` |

2250.content:
| Components                    | Instance                                    |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Some components are `UNKNOWN` | `DEGRADED` (`UNKNOWN` when all are unknown) |

2251.content:
| Components                          | Instance      |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------- |
| All components are in `MAINTENANCE` | `MAINTENANCE` |

2253.content:
Services and databases are critical by default. Caches, queues and storage are not. A template can
change this per resource with the `critical` field.

2254.content:
Each tenant has a **private status page**, at `/status/<tenantId>` in the console. It groups
resources into components that customers see: API, Workers, Database, Cache, Messaging, Storage,
and DNS & TLS. The headline shows the worst component state.

2261.content:
Members of the tenant and platform staff can read the page. Public pages and status subscriptions
are on the roadmap.

2262.content: Alert rules are stored as data. OrkStage seeds two of them:

2263.content:
| Rule                          | Opens an incident after         | Severity | Cooldown   |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------- | -------- | ---------- |
| `Critical resource unhealthy` | 3 failed health checks in a row | high     | 15 minutes |

2264.content:
| Rule                              | Opens an incident after         | Severity | Cooldown   |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | -------- | ---------- |
| `Non-critical resource unhealthy` | 5 failed health checks in a row | medium   | 30 minutes |

2266.content:
They are **deduplicated** per resource. A resource has at most one open incident, so a flapping
resource never opens many.

2267.content:
After an incident resolves, a **cooldown** passes before a new one can open for the same
resource.

2268.content: They are **resolved automatically** when health returns, with a final update.

2269.content:
Platform staff (owners, admins and operators) can open an incident by hand and post updates. Each
update has a status, a message and an optional impact. Tenant members can read incidents and their
updates, which appear on the incident page in order. Through the API, this needs the
`incidents:write` scope.

2270.content: The data model includes maintenance windows, but no screen schedules them yet.

2272.content: Create, clone, validate and publish OrkStage templates in the console, in the YAML editor or the drag and drop builder that edits the same document.

2277.content:
Platform staff manage templates: owners and admins publish them, and operators can read them.
Tenants use published versions when they create instances.

2278.content: **New template** creates the first version as a draft.

2279.content: **New version** adds a draft version. Published versions are never edited.

2280.content: **Publish** runs the full validation and refuses unsafe templates.

2281.content: **Clone** copies a template under a new name, for example to start from a predefined one.

2282.content: An instance keeps its version until someone runs **Upgrade template** on it.

2283.content: Validation runs in stages and reports every issue with its stage, severity, code and path:

2284.content:
| Stage    | Checks                                                                     |
| -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `schema` | YAML syntax and the `platform/v1` schema (types, ranges, required fields). |

2285.content:
| Stage      | Checks                                                                                                |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `semantic` | Unique ids, valid references (`dependsOn`, routes, DNS target, variables), existing slots, no cycles. |

2286.content:
| Stage  | Checks                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `plan` | The template is offered on each plan it lists and fits that plan's entitlements: limits on services, vCPU, memory, replicas, database storage and custom domains, plus autoscaling and backup retention. |

2287.content:
| Stage        | Checks                                                                             |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `capability` | The providers each slot allows can implement every resource. Includes suggestions. |

2288.content:
| Stage    | Checks                                                       |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `policy` | Governance policies that can be checked without an instance. |

2289.content:
CI can run the same validation without storing anything: `POST /templates/validate` (see
CI/CD intake).

2290.content:
To open the builder, choose **Templates**, then **New**, then **Builder**, or click **Builder** on
an existing template. It is a drag and drop canvas:

2291.content: Drag resource types from the palette onto the canvas.

2292.content: Placement slots are lanes. Drop a resource into a lane to place it, and add or remove lanes.

2293.content: Connect nodes to add dependencies and connectivity requirements, with protocol, port and mode.

2294.content: Edit each resource's fields in the side panel, under the same constraints as the schema.

2295.content:
The builder edits **the same YAML document** you see in the source view and validates it as you
work, so you can switch between the two at any time.

2296.content:
The template reference describes the full format. If you
keep templates in a repository, the `ork` CLI pushes them as new versions
(Preview). IaC import can draft a template from existing
Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes or Compose files.

2298.content: Run provider actions on a deployed instance (redeploy, restart, rollback, purge cache, backup) by hand, from CI with an API key, or on a schedule.

2303.content:
Triggers are declared in the template (reference)
and apply to every instance built from it. Each one runs a single action on a single resource
through the provider that owns it, so the action and its parameters depend on the provider: a
Vercel project offers `redeploy`, `promote`, `rollback` and `purge-cache`; a Render service offers
`redeploy`, `restart`, `rollback`, `scale`, `suspend` and `resume`; a Supabase database offers
`restart`, `pause`, `restore` and `backup`; a Cloud Run or Container Apps service offers `redeploy`
or `restart`.

2304.content:
A trigger starts work at the provider and records the result: the provider deployment or backup
it started, a link when there is one, and a message. It does not wait for a build to finish; the
instance health and the provider deployment history show how that ends.

2305.content:
Open the instance and choose **Triggers**. Each trigger shows the resource and action, how it can
run (manual, API key, schedule) and its last result. **Run** opens the parameters the template
marks as overridable; everything else keeps its template value. Running a trigger needs the
deploy permission on the instance.

2306.content:
A trigger is unavailable while its resource is not deployed, or when the provider of that
resource does not offer the action (for example a template that asks for `backup` on a provider
without on demand backups). The console shows the reason.

2307.content:
Triggers with `on.webhook: true` accept calls from an API key with
the `instances:deploy` scope:

2308.content:
The call returns `202` with the run (`status: QUEUED`). Parameters that are not overridable,
unknown to the action or of the wrong type are rejected with `422` before anything reaches the
provider. A trigger without `on.webhook` refuses API keys with `403`.

2309.content:
`on.schedule` takes a five field cron expression in UTC. The worker keeps one schedule per
trigger and instance, replaces it after every deployment (so a changed or removed schedule takes
effect with the next deploy) and removes it when the instance is destroyed. Scheduled runs are
skipped while the instance is not `READY` or `DEGRADED`.

2310.content:
Every run is stored with its source (`MANUAL`, `SCHEDULE`, `WEBHOOK`), parameters, status and
result, and appears under **Recent runs** and in `GET /instances/{id}/trigger-runs`. Runs are
audited, and their outcome is sent as the `trigger.succeeded` and `trigger.failed`
notification and webhook events.

orderedDocs:
"OrkStage" and the OrkStage logo are trademarks of the project. Forks must use a different name and
logo. The trademark policy lists what is fine, what needs permission and what is not
allowed.
[ ] `NODE_ENV=production`, dev login off and an OIDC provider configured.
[ ] `SESSION_SECRET` and `ENCRYPTION_KEY` generated at random and injected from a secret store.

**A clear boundary.** Core code never imports from `ee/`. Enterprise features plug into extension
points. Without a license that covers them, gated endpoints answer `402 ENTERPRISE_REQUIRED`.

**A license key turns it on.** Set `ORKSTAGE_LICENSE_KEY` to the key you receive. The key is a
signed token (Ed25519) that OrkStage verifies **offline**. OrkStage does not contact a license
server and does not require usage reports.

**Accepted.** `CloudProviderAdapter` is the only way the platform touches a cloud. Its
`ensureResource` call converges a resource to the desired state, so a retry cannot create a
duplicate.

**Accepted.** All tenants share one database, and every row a tenant owns carries a `tenantId`.
Isolation works in four layers: the request principal, query scoping by membership, a CASL check
on the loaded record, and the audit log. A record from another tenant is reported as not found.

**Accepted.** Every `tofu` command runs in a throwaway container with a pinned image. Credentials
exist only in that container's environment.

**Accepted.** Templates are shared across tenants, but each tenant has its own cloud accounts. So
the provider, account and region cannot live in the template.

**Accepted.** Temporal would add a cluster to operate. BullMQ reuses the Redis and Postgres that
the platform already requires.

**Application platforms** (Vercel, Render and Supabase) are driven through their **REST APIs**.
There is no OpenTofu, no module and no state store: the platform itself holds the state, and the
adapter finds its resources again by name, so repeating a deployment converges the existing
resource instead of creating a second one.
**Audit log**: every change, filtered by tenant (`GET /audit`).

**Audit**: every action a key takes is recorded with `actorType = API_KEY` and
`actorLabel = "<key name> (<prefix>)"`.

**AWS** reads the bucket key from the Secrets Manager secret the module created in your
account, using the deployment role.

**Backend**: S3, with `use_lockfile` for locking, and encryption. On real AWS, you create the bucket
in advance with versioning and encryption, and OrkStage validates it before use (see
Connecting an AWS account). On an
emulator, OrkStage creates the bucket on first use.

**Cancel** stops the deployment cooperatively. The worker checks for the request while it runs,
and resources that have not started yet are marked cancelled.

**Change template version** shows the plan from what runs now to the chosen version (what is
created, updated and deleted), then starts a deployment of that version. The instance keeps its
current version until that deployment succeeds, so a failed upgrade leaves it on the version that
actually runs; **Retry** continues the upgrade. Choosing an older version rolls back the same way.
Production upgrades that delete or replace resources wait for approval. An instance never changes
version on its own.

**CLI.** A tag publishes signed `ork` binaries for Linux (glibc and musl), macOS and Windows on
`x86_64` and `arm64`, then `@orkstage/scan` on npm, then manifests for Homebrew, Scoop and
winget.

**Clone and customize** (template authors) copies the template so you can change it in the
builder and publish your own version.
**Clone** copies a template under a new name, for example to start from a predefined one.

**Community** is complete. It includes templates, multicloud placement, plans, policies and cost,
deployments, health, incidents, status pages, notifications, the audit log, API keys, webhooks, CI
intake, IaC import and the CLI. **Enterprise** adds features for organizational scale and
compliance.

**Compatibility matrix.** `orkstage-dev/COMPATIBILITY.md` lists the combination of versions
that was tested together. Its CI runs the end to end suite against that combination.

**Connections** inferred from references, for example a task definition that reads the database
address.

**Console.** A tag publishes `ghcr.io/orkstage/console:<version>`, pinned to a compatible range
of the contracts package.

**Copy as Mermaid** copies the same diagram as a Mermaid flowchart, ready for a design document or
a pull request description.

**Deployments** lists every deployment across the instances you can see. A deployment page shows
the step list, a Gantt timeline, the plan and the event log. When they apply, it also shows
**Approve**, **Cancel** and **Retry**.

**Deployments**: every step with its duration, attempts and failure class, plus the event log and
the Gantt timeline.
**Destroy** removes every cloud resource in reverse dependency order:

**Detect** each source kind. Terraform is parsed as HCL. The scan evaluates `var.*`, `local.*`
and simple expressions, expands local modules per call and reports remote modules as unmapped.
References such as `aws_db_instance.main.address` in a task definition become connections.
CloudFormation tags in short form (such as `!Ref`, `!GetAtt` and `!Sub`) are normalized.

**Development login**: an email only login for local installs. It is off unless
`AUTH_DEV_LOGIN_ENABLED=true`, and the API refuses to start with it on when
`NODE_ENV=production`.
**Docker**, for Postgres, Redis, Mailpit, MiniStack and the OpenTofu runner containers.

**Edition at a glance.** `GET /api/v1/license` reports the active edition and features, and the
console shows an edition badge.

**Engineering managers** who approve production changes. They see the plan, the risk and an
approximate cost before anything is created.

**Expiry**: `expiresAt` is optional and must be in the future. An expired key gets
`401 INVALID_API_KEY`.

**Health checks** roll up to the instance. They open **incidents**, update a private **status
page** and send **notifications**. Every change is recorded in an **audit log** that only accepts
inserts.
**Incidents** lists open and resolved incidents with their updates.

**Infer**. The scan adds a network when services or data stores need one, and an ingress plus DNS
for a public HTTP service on a cloud provider. It then chooses placement slots and the smallest
plan whose default entitlements fit.

**Infrastructure clouds** (AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure,
DigitalOcean, Vultr, CoreWeave and Magalu Cloud) are deployed with **OpenTofu**. For each resource,
the worker runs an OpenTofu module in a throwaway runner container. Every resource has its own
state file, kept in a bucket or container **in your own account**. OrkStage keeps outputs and
references, not the state.
**Last use**: the API updates `lastUsedAt` and the client address at most once a minute.

**Merge**. When several sources show the same component, it becomes one resource that keeps
every source. IaC evidence wins over Kubernetes, and Kubernetes wins over Compose, Dockerfiles and
package hints.

**Modules.** Git tags `vX.Y.Z` publish `ghcr.io/orkstage/tofu-runner:<tag>`. The platform pins
the runner tag, so a module change is always an explicit upgrade.
**New template** creates the first version as a draft.
**New version** adds a draft version. Published versions are never edited.

**Node.js 24 or later** and **pnpm 12**. Run `corepack enable` to get the pnpm version pinned in
`package.json`.

**One codebase, one build.** Enterprise code lives in directories named `ee/` and ships in the
same images. There is no separate fork.

**OrkStage places each resource on its own.** One instance can run its API on AWS, its database on
Azure and its storage on OCI.
**Overview**: instances, deployments, failures and incidents, with trends.

**Platform and DevOps teams** that run the same environment shape for many customers or teams.
They get one reviewed path from template to cloud, with policy checks on every plan.

**Platform.** A tag builds and publishes `ghcr.io/orkstage/platform:<version>` and the shared
packages (`@orkstage/contracts`, `/authorization`, `/templates` and `/domain`). The exported
OpenAPI document is attached to the release.

**Precedence**: flags first, then environment variables, then `.ork/config.toml`, then the user
config.

**Production use requires a subscription.** A license key turns on the features you subscribed
to.
**Publish** runs the full validation and refuses unsafe templates.

**Render and validate** the template. Problems become warnings, so the scan never fails on bad
input.

**Resources**: each detected resource with its OrkStage type, provider, implementation,
confidence (`high`, `medium` or `low`) and the source evidence, such as
`main.tf:12 aws_db_instance.main`.

**Retry** runs only the failed and skipped resources again. Resources that already converged are
left alone.

**Revocation**: call `DELETE /api/v1/api-keys/:id` (it returns `204`) or use the console. The key
stops working at once and also gets `401 INVALID_API_KEY`.

**Settings > Team** lists the members of a tenant with their roles, and the invitations still
pending. Owners (and platform staff) invite people by email with a role:

**simulates the role** against the actions each supported service needs, with
`iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy`.

**Single sign on**: every provider configured with OIDC appears on the login page. Microsoft Entra
ID is the reference provider, and you can add any other OIDC provider through configuration. See
Configuration.

**Site.** This site refreshes the API reference from the release's OpenAPI file and deploys to
S3 and CloudFront.

**SREs** who need health, incidents, status and an audit trail tied to the infrastructure that
was actually deployed.
**Star** keeps a listing in mind and helps others find popular ones.

**Supabase** derives the database password again from the OrkStage encryption key. It is never
stored anywhere: it was derived the same way when the project was created.

**Templates**, then **Import**, turns existing infrastructure code into a draft template. The
OrkStage scan engine detects and maps the resources. It is the same engine the `ork` CLI uses.

**The database password is never stored.** OrkStage derives it from its encryption key (an HMAC
of `supabase:db:<target id>:<project name>`). The adapter turns that into a 32 character
alphanumeric password, sends it once when it creates the project, and derives it again whenever
it is needed.
**Unmapped** items: what the engine saw but cannot express in a template, with the reason.

**Use this template** opens the instance wizard with the template and its published version
already selected; you choose the tenant, bind each placement slot to your cloud targets and set
the variables. Templates that need more than one provider require a plan with multiple
providers (GROWTH or SCALE).
**versioning enabled**, so you can recover from a damaged state;

**Versioning.** Each repository uses semantic versions. A breaking API change gets a new
`/api/v2` route group. The template schema has its own version (`platform/v1`).

**Walk** (CLI only). A parallel walk that respects `.gitignore` skips `node_modules`,
`.terraform`, `target`, `vendor`, `dist`, hidden directories and CDK `asset.*` copies. It also
skips files over 1 MiB (configurable) and files that are not valid UTF-8.
**Warnings** and the **validation** result of the generated template.
**Webhook deliveries**: status, attempts and the last error of each endpoint.

**Your data stays usable.** Without a key, or with an invalid key, OrkStage runs as Community. When
a key expires, a banner shows a 14 day grace period, after which Enterprise features switch off.
OrkStage never deletes or locks your data.

`accessKeys: true` on `files` matters here: a Vercel app cannot assume an AWS role, so the AWS
module creates an access key limited to this one bucket for it.

`allowedRegions` and `defaultRegion` are CoreWeave zone names such as `US-EAST-04A`. VPCs and
buckets are created in the deployment region. A VPC lives in one zone.

`autoscaling` creates a HorizontalPodAutoscaler on CPU. The Deployment then leaves the replica
count to it.

`CloudProviderAdapter` is the only way the platform touches a cloud. It defines `validateTarget`,
`capabilities`, an idempotent `ensureResource`, `deleteResource`, `getResource` and `checkHealth`, plus
optional logs, metrics, plan and existence probes. One shared contract test suite runs against every
adapter.

`config` holds only identifiers that are not secret. The API rejects keys that look like secrets
with `422 SECRET_IN_CONFIG`. After registering, click **Validate**: each adapter checks the
configuration, signs in and shows the identity it found. Infrastructure clouds also check that
the state storage answers.

`config` must not contain secrets. The API rejects keys that look like secrets with
`422 SECRET_IN_CONFIG`. `credentialRef` must be an `env://` or `aws-sm://` reference, and any other
value is rejected. You can assign a target to one tenant (`tenantId`) or share it across tenants.
`cpu` and `memoryMiB` become resource requests. Memory is also the limit.
`database` and `files` publish only a reference in their outputs (`secret_ref`), never a value.
`digest` must be `sha256:` followed by 64 lowercase hex characters.

`docker-compose.yml` in the `orkstage-dev` workspace
runs the whole platform from one shared image, built from the repositories checked out as
submodules. It is the supported way to evaluate OrkStage and the starting point for an
installation on a single host. Run the commands on this page from the `orkstage-dev` checkout.

`env://` references cannot read the platform's own configuration (`DATABASE_URL`, `REDIS_URL`,
`SESSION_SECRET`, `ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `ORKSTAGE_LICENSE_KEY` and anything starting with `OIDC_`,
`SMTP_`, `AWS_`, `TOFU_`, `API_`, `WEB_`, `APP_` or `NODE_`). Give target credentials their own
names, for example `ORK_AZURE_CREDENTIALS`.
`env` is `live` or `test`. It is a label for you, and both kinds work the same way.

`fumadocs-openapi` generates these pages from `openapi/orkstage.json`, the document a running API
serves at `/api/docs-json`. The interactive Swagger UI is at `/api/docs`. Read the
REST API overview first for authentication, errors, pagination and
correlation ids.
`GET /healthz` and `GET /readyz` have no limit. A `429` response means wait and retry with backoff.

`GET /me` returns the caller, their memberships and the authorization rules. When you call it with an
API key, it also returns `apiKey: { id, name, prefix, scopes }`.

`kubeconfig`: only for clusters reached another way (a private endpoint, a different token).
The current context's server, `certificate-authority-data` and bearer `token` are used. Client
certificates and exec plugins are not supported.

`on.schedule` takes a five field cron expression in UTC. The worker keeps one schedule per
trigger and instance, replaces it after every deployment (so a changed or removed schedule takes
effect with the next deploy) and removes it when the instance is destroyed. Scheduled runs are
skipped while the instance is not `READY` or `DEGRADED`.
`ork import` scans on your machine, sends only the report, and prints a console link:
`ork init` leaves one line per placement slot to fill in `.ork/config.toml`:

`ork` turns an existing project into an OrkStage template, pushes it, and deploys and operates
instances from your terminal or from CI. It reads Terraform and OpenTofu, CloudFormation, SAM and
CDK, Kubernetes and Helm, Docker Compose, Dockerfiles and package manifests. It also detects Pulumi,
Serverless, Bicep and ARM projects. The CLI is written in Rust and licensed under AGPL-3.0.

`OrkStage-Delivery` is unique per delivery and stays the same across retries. A manual redelivery is
a new delivery with a new `OrkStage-Delivery` value, but its body keeps the original `id`. To drop
duplicates, use the body `id`, which covers both retries and redeliveries.

`orkstage-dev` is the workspace that brings the repositories together as git submodules: the
control plane, the console, the CLI, the OpenTofu modules and this site.

`orkstage/` (the core) is a normal clone with its own pnpm workspace and lockfile. Inside it,
every command works as in a standalone checkout. It does not use Turborepo: `pnpm -r` already
runs scripts in dependency order (see
ADR 0006). All code is ESM
TypeScript 7 with `module: NodeNext`.
`orkstage/platform:local`, shared by the API, the worker, the console and the `migrate` job.
`orkstage/tofu-runner:local`, which contains OpenTofu 1.12.7 and the OpenTofu modules.

`public: true` creates a `LoadBalancer` Service with the
`service.beta.kubernetes.io/coreweave-load-balancer-type: public` annotation. The module waits
for the public IP and outputs `url`.

`purge-cache` with `*` relies on the project wide tag. Purges by tag need responses tagged with
`Vercel-Cache-Tag`.

`readSecret` answers `vultr-db://<id>` and `vultr-objstore://<id>` from the Vultr API (the public
host when there is one), so a frontend on another provider can be wired to them.
`redeploy` and `rollback` return the Render deploy id as the action reference.

`scanFiles(files, options?)` is synchronous and does no I/O. The options are `templateName`,
`displayName`, `templateVersion` and `maxFileBytes`.

`stateAccessKeyId` and `stateSecretAccessKey`: an AI Object Storage access key that can read and
write the state bucket and the buckets OrkStage creates.

`supabase://<ref>/storage` returns `url` (project API URL), `serviceRoleKey` and `anonKey`,
read from the Management API each time.

`token`: a CoreWeave API access token (Console, Tokens). The OpenTofu runner receives it as
`COREWEAVE_API_TOKEN`. CKS managed auth accepts the same token as a Kubernetes bearer token, so
with `clusterName` set no kubeconfig is needed: the adapter looks up the cluster's API server
endpoint through the CKS API.

| OIDC | Authorization code grant with PKCE (S256). `state` and `nonce` are verified. The flow state lives in a signed, short lived cookie. `returnTo` accepts relative paths only. Provider tokens are discarded. |

| Phase                                      | What happens                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Remove resources no longer in the template | Deletes resources the instance still has but the template no longer contains (after an upgrade, or a resource turned off by a variable), dependents first. The plan lists them as deletions, so production approval covers them. A destroy protected instance keeps them, with a warning. |

| Phase                                | What happens                                                        |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Health and connectivity verification | Checks each resource until it is healthy, within one settle window. |

| Phase                             | What happens                                                         |
| --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Configure secrets and connections | Wires connection references. Secret values stay in the secret store. |

| Phase                            | What happens                                                          |
| -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Register observability, Finalize | Registers monitoring and moves the instance to `READY` or `DEGRADED`. |

| Phase                          | What happens                                                                      |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Validate template and policies | The stored snapshot is checked again. A failing policy stops the deployment here. |

| Phase                  | What happens                                                                                           |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Validate cloud targets | Checks credentials, the state bucket and, on real AWS, the IAM permissions the deployed services need. |

| Phase               | What happens                                                                      |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Application rollout | Services run their images by digest, so the exact image never changes under them. |

| Phase         | What happens                                                                               |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Generate plan | Builds the platform diff, plus a real `tofu plan` for each existing resource that changes. |

| Phase     | What happens                                                                      |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Resources | One step per resource, in dependency order. Independent branches run in parallel. |

| Phase    | What happens                                                                                      |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Approval | Runs only for high risk production changes (see below). Otherwise it is skipped, with the reason. |

A **cloud target** is an account you register with a provider: an AWS account, an Azure
subscription or an OCI tenancy. It stores the allowed regions and configuration that is not secret.
Credentials are stored as references, never as values.

A **deployment** applies a plan in the background. The worker runs fixed phases: validate, targets,
plan, approval (when needed), resources, rollout, configure, verify, observability and finalize.
A **deployment** applies the plan in the background with OpenTofu, following the dependency graph.

A **template** (`apiVersion: platform/v1`, `kind: EnvironmentTemplate`) describes business intent,
never provider resource blocks. Examples: "a container service with two replicas", "a Postgres
database spread across availability zones", "private connectivity from api to database".

A **template** describes what the environment needs, without naming a provider. You write it
once and deploy it many times.
A `fail` result blocks the deployment. Custom templates go through the same policies.

A template declares **placement slots** such as `primary`, `data` and `storage`, and lists the
providers each slot accepts. Every resource names a slot, and an instance binds each slot to a target
and a region. Bind all slots to one AWS account and the template runs on a single cloud. Bind `data`
to Azure and the same template becomes multicloud.

A template describes **intent**, never provider resource blocks. The schema on this page comes from
`packages/templates/src/schema.ts`, the source of truth for the API, the console builder and the
CLI.

A template lists the plans it supports. The compiler refuses a placement the plan does not allow,
for example a second provider when `multiCloud` is off.

A template names resource types such as `database.postgresql` or `web.frontend`, never a provider.
When you create an instance, each placement slot is bound to a **cloud target** (one account,
project, team or workspace of a provider) and a region. The provider adapter behind that target
turns each resource into real infrastructure.

A tenant's **plan** (`FREE`, `SANDBOX`, `STARTER`, `GROWTH` or `SCALE`) grants **entitlements**.
Some are limits: instances, services, CPU, memory, storage, replicas, domains and retention. Others
are switches: custom templates, custom cloud accounts, several regions, several clouds and
autoscaling.

A trigger is a named action on one deployed resource, with default parameters: redeploy a
frontend, restart a service, take a database restore point. The provider decides which actions
exist; the console and `GET /instances/{id}/triggers` list them with their parameters.

A trigger is unavailable while its resource is not deployed, or when the provider of that
resource does not offer the action (for example a template that asks for `backup` on a provider
without on demand backups). The console shows the reason.

A trigger starts work at the provider and records the result: the provider deployment or backup
it started, a link when there is one, and a message. It does not wait for a build to finish; the
instance health and the provider deployment history show how that ends.

validation; create one ingress per service. TLS needs a domain that already points at the load
balancer (`overrides.vultr.autoSslDomain`). Without it the load balancer serves HTTP only.

An **instance** binds each placement slot of the template to a cloud target and a region.

An **instance**, also called a **stage**, is one isolated, logical environment for one tenant. It
holds the services, database, cache, queue, storage, ingress and DNS, for example *Acme Production*
or *Acme Staging*. Each instance has an environment kind (`production`, `staging`, `development` or
`sandbox`), a template version, variable values and one placement binding per slot.

An **organization** runs one OrkStage installation. It serves **tenants**, the customers or teams
that own instances. Every record that belongs to a tenant carries its tenant id. A user sees a
tenant only through a membership with one of the roles. Each tenant is
on a **plan**.

An API key acts **with a role**. A tenant key uses `CustomerAdmin`, `CustomerDeveloper` or
`CustomerViewer`. A key for the whole organization uses `PlatformAdmin` or `PlatformOperator`.
Scopes then narrow what the role allows, so a key can never do more than its role.

pending changes. A new deployment restores the configuration from the template.

The **Metrics** tab charts CPU, memory, requests per minute, p95 latency and errors per minute for

The **Overview** tab of an instance draws its topology. Every resource is a node, grouped by
provider, target and region. Dependency edges connect the nodes, and connectivity links carry the
strategy label, for example `public-tls-allowlist` between AWS and Azure. Node colors follow
health, and simulated resources carry a *simulated* label.

The **Plan & cost** tab of an instance runs a preview (`POST /instances/:id/preview`). The preview
compiles the template with the instance's variables and placements, then compares the result with
what OrkStage already knows about the instance. It never touches a cloud and saves nothing.

The **plan** resolves every resource, evaluates policies, estimates the monthly cost and picks a
connectivity strategy for each link between clouds. No cloud is touched at this step.

The **provider plan** deletes or replaces something. This is a real `tofu plan`, run for each
changed resource during the plan phase. It can find a replacement even when the platform diff
shows only an update, for example when an attribute forces replacement. Routine ECS task
definition revisions do not count.

The **Validate cloud targets** phase repeats these checks for each target and region the deployment
uses. This time it checks only the services being deployed, and it is strict. A missing permission
fails the phase with `AUTHORIZATION_ERROR` before any resource is touched, and the error names the
missing actions.

Values never appear in outputs, logs or error messages. Errors from Supabase are redacted.

Values never appear in outputs, logs or error messages. The adapter owns the environment of the
services it manages: variables added by hand in the dashboard are replaced on the next apply.
Changes to settings or variables start one deploy so they take effect.

Variable names come from the resource id: `database` becomes `DATABASE`, `files` becomes `FILES`
(upper case, any other character turned into `_`). Connection settings from outputs are added as
`<ID>_HOST`, `<ID>_PORT`, `<ID>_URL`, `<ID>_BUCKET`, `<ID>_ENDPOINT` and `<ID>_REGION`. Each
credential field becomes `<ID>_<FIELD>`, with camel case turned into upper snake case
(`poolerUrl` becomes `POOLER_URL`, `secretAccessKey` becomes `SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`). When a name
comes from both, the credential wins and the variable is stored as sensitive.

Verification waits in **one settle window of 5 minutes per deployment**, not one per resource, so a
slow service does not multiply the wait.

Versions are immutable. Publishing a version again with the **same** digest is idempotent (the
response has `"idempotent": true`). With a different digest it fails with `409 VERSION_EXISTS`.

and `availabilityZones` does not create more subnets.

When that happens, OrkStage marks the resource `DRIFT_DETECTED` with the planned actions, writes an
audit event and notifies owners and admins (`instance.drift_detected`). Resources with a pending
change are skipped, because that change is a deployment, not drift. **Deploy** restores the
template's configuration.

`Not needed: no high-risk or destructive changes planned.` Instances in other environments
(`staging`, `development`, `sandbox`) never wait for approval.
